He should rather seek the protection of Allah and pray to Him, for He is the One who can keep a servant safe from errors and sins. Willpower is not the safeguard. Allah is.

Notice also the shape of the rebuke itself. Maʿārif points out that the stern response was followed by a mollifying remark — the good counsel was being given to him so that he too would not become one of the ignorant. Protection offered, not condemnation issued.

## Down the mountain, and how far the peace reaches

Only after the correction and the repentance does the command to disembark arrive. Ibn Kathir places it at the moment the ship anchored on Mount Jūdī: peace was sent upon Nuh, peace be upon him, and upon the believers with him.

Maʿārif fills in the picture. The flood subsided, the ark came to rest on Mount Jūdiyy, the earth sucked its water back, and the standing water from the heaven was preserved in the form of rivers and streams, making the land habitable again. Nuh (peace be upon him) was then asked to disembark and go down the mountain, for there was nothing to worry about: the blessings of Allah would be with him, keeping him secure from calamities and hardships, and he would prosper in terms of peace, wealth and children.

**And here the circle opens.** In ayah 46 the promise was narrowed until it excluded a son. In ayah 48 it is widened until it includes people not yet born. Ibn Kathir reports that this salutation was also for every believer from Nuh's progeny until the Day of Resurrection. Muḥammad bin Kaʿb said: "Every male and female believer until the Day of Resurrection is included in this salutation of peace. Likewise, every male and female disbeliever until the Day of Resurrection is included in this promise of torment and pleasure."

Maʿārif reaches the same conclusion from the wording. The promise of peace and blessing is not limited to Nuh's person; it was said **"and upon the peoples springing from those with you."** Those who boarded the ark are identified by the word *umam*, the plural of *ummah* (community) — although we already know that those aboard were mostly people from Nuh's own family plus a few other believers. They are named as different communities because different communities and nationalities would spring forth from their future generations. On this basis the entire post-flood human population of the world is his progeny, which is why the Qurʼan says elsewhere, **"and those remaining We made his descendants"** (37:77), and why historians refer to him as the second Adam.

**Why the verse then turns to warning.** Since those coming generations would include believers and disbelievers both, the subject of peace and blessing had to be elaborated. For believers it is correct in its general sense: peace and blessing in the mortal world and in the Hereafter. But the disbelievers of that same progeny would be consigned to lasting punishment. Hence the close of the ayah: "And there are peoples whom We shall give some enjoyment, then a painful punishment from Us will visit them." Maʿārif's image is exact: the peace and blessing of this world is like a feast thrown open to all, friends and foes alike, and those who take to disbelief eat at that table too. But the salvation and prosperity of the Hereafter is reserved for believers. The disbeliever is given the return for his good deeds within the mortal world, and there is nothing left for him to receive afterwards.

**A note on the well-known details.** Ibn Kathir transmits from Muḥammad bin Isḥāq that when Allah wanted to stop the flood, He sent a wind upon the face of the earth that caused the water to be still; the springs of the earth were closed off and the pouring rain from the sky halted — "O earth! Swallow up your water" (11:44) — until the ship settled on Mount Jūdī. What follows in that report is a detailed chronology which Ibn Kathir expressly attributes to the People of the Tawrah: months counted off, the mountain tops appearing, a raven sent out that did not return, a pigeon that came back having found no place to put its two feet down, a second sending that returned in the evening with a leaf from an olive tree in its mouth, and a third from which it did not return at all, so Nuh knew that the earth had appeared. Ibn Kathir names the source of these details rather than asserting them — reported material from the earlier scripture, not something the Qurʼan itself states.

## Why the Prophet ﷺ is being told all this

"This is of the news of the Unseen which We reveal unto you; neither you nor your people knew it before this."

Ibn Kathir explains: this is from the information of the unseen of the past, revealed to the Prophet ﷺ *in the way that it occurred, as if he witnessed it himself.* "We reveal it unto you" means: We teach it to you as revelation from Us. And "neither you nor your people knew it before this" is there so that **no one who rejects him can say he learned it from them.** Rather, it was Allah who informed him of it, in conformity with the true situation — just as the Books of the Prophets before him testify.

Maʿārif spells the argument out in full. The flood lay in the domain of the unseen. The Prophet ﷺ had no knowledge of it beforehand, nor did his people, the Arabs; he is the one who told them about it. Had his people been educated and conversant with world history, one might surmise that he had heard these events from the learned among them. But his whole people were unaware of them, and he had never gone to another country to get an education there. The only inlet for this knowledge therefore stands determined conclusively: *waḥy*, divine revelation — a clear proof that he is a true messenger of Allah. The story he relates becomes a standing witness to the veracity of the one relating it.

**And then, patience.** "So be patient. Surely, the good end is for those who have taqwa." *Taqwa* is the fear of Allah — the quality Maʿārif names alongside faith and goodness as the thing everything in religion functionally depends on. Ibn Kathir reads the command as a direct address to the Prophet ﷺ: be patient with the rejection of your people and their harming you, for We shall help you and surround you with Our aid, and We will make the good end yours and the good end of those who follow you, in this life and the Hereafter — as We did with the Messengers when We helped them against their enemies. He brings two ayat as witnesses to that standing rule: **"Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe"** (40:51), and **"And, verily, Our Word has gone forth of old for Our servants, the Messengers, that they verily, would be made triumphant"** (37:171–172).

Maʿārif adds the consolation in human terms. If there are some unfortunate human beings who see the sun and yet insist that they do not, who challenge and confront him, then the Prophet ﷺ should look at the role model of his predecessor, Nuh (peace be upon him), who spent one thousand years of his long life suffering pain inflicted by his people, and remained patient. It stands determined that success will ultimately kiss the hands of those who are patient and who fear Allah.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer:

- **Check before you pray.** Find out first whether what you are asking for is permissible and lawful. Making duʿāʼ under doubtful circumstances is prohibited; praying for what is known to be impermissible is all the more so.
- **Do not lean on your own resolve after a mistake.** Nuh's response in ayah 47 is not a promise to do better; it is seeking refuge in Allah, asking forgiveness, asking for mercy. That is the model Maʿārif tells us to copy.
- **Let your loyalties run along faith, not blood — and let your kindness run wider than your loyalties.** Kinship carries no weight in religious and collective matters, as ayah 46 establishes. But good social behaviour, moral grace, favour and generosity toward those outside that circle are permissible, recommended, and worthy of reward.

And the last word of the passage is the one to keep: the good end belongs to those who have taqwa. Nuh (peace be upon him) lost a son to the water — and still walked down that mountain under a greeting of peace that, Ibn Kathir tells us, reaches every believer until the Day of Resurrection.

passages.title: Hūd calls 'Ad to their Lord alone
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat open the story of Hud, peace be upon him, the prophet sent to the people of 'Ad — and they contain his entire message in three moves. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān numbers them as the three basic principles of his call: worship Allah alone, because everything else you worship is your own invention (ayah 50); I am a messenger who asks you for nothing (ayah 51); so seek forgiveness and turn back, and watch what your Lord does for you (ayah 52). Read together they are a complete model of how a prophet speaks to his people.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this sūrah carries the stories of seven prophets, from Sayyidnā Nuh to Sayyidnā Musa, peace be upon them, told in the Qur'an's own unmistakable style — accounts that carry "such flashes of lesson and advice that no one with a responsive and discerning heart can remain unaffected by them." They are not only moral tales: they contain principles of faith and right action, and guidance a believer can apply in comparable situations of his own. Of all seven prophets mentioned, it is Hud, peace be upon him, whose name the sūrah bears — which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, shows that his story carries a particular significance here. His portion runs across ayat 50–60, and these three are its opening.

**A detail worth noticing.** Ayah 50 carries no stated verb of sending — literally, "And to 'Ad, their brother Hud." Ibn Kathir explains that the opening "And" (*wa*) "is an introductory to what is implied: 'Verily, We sent.'" The words the commentary supplies name the One behind the sending; the ayah's own words move straight to the people and to the man who came to them.

## "Their brother Hud"

Allah does not say "a warner" or "a man" but *akhāhum*, **their brother**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this establishes: Hud, peace be upon him, was one of them, from their own stock. The people of 'Ad, it explains, "were known for their physical build, strength and bravery" — a people who had every worldly reason for confidence. And here lies the tragedy the commentary underlines: a people so strong and so brave "had lost their reason to the extent that they had taken to worshipping gods they had carved out of stones with their own hands."

Hold those two facts together and the passage begins to breathe. The strongest people of their age were bowing to stone. The man sent to correct them was not a foreign critic but their own kinsman, who knew them and shared their lineage.

## Ayah 50: the whole of religion in one sentence

"Worship Allah! You have no other god but Him." This is *tawḥīd* — the Oneness of Allah, that He alone is worthy of worship. Ibn Kathir summarises the mission in exactly these terms: Hud, peace be upon him, came "commanding them to worship Allah alone, without any associates," and he "forbade them from worshipping the idols which they made up, inventing names as gods."

Notice the double invention Ibn Kathir describes. Their hands made the objects; their tongues supplied the names and the divinity. That is why the ayah closes as it does: **"Certainly, you do nothing but invent lies."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this the first principle of the call — belief in the Oneness of Allah, "and that taking someone or something else worthy of worship other than Allah is nothing but a lie and fabrication."

That is a sharper charge than "you are mistaken." A mistake can be inherited innocently; a fabrication is something you manufactured. Hud, peace be upon him, is telling a proud people that the religion they defend so fiercely is a thing they made — no more ancient, no more authoritative, and no more powerful than the hands that carved it.

## Ayah 51: the messenger who wants nothing from you

Having stated the claim, Hud, peace be upon him, immediately removes the obvious suspicion: **what is he getting out of this?** "O my people, I ask of you no reward for it. My reward is only from Him Who created me."

Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: he "informed them that he did not want any reward from them for his sincere advising and conveying of Allah's Message. He only sought his reward from Allah, the One Who created him." The One who brought him into being is the One he looks to for payment; his people are owed no share in his motives.

Then comes the closing question of the ayah: *"Will you not then understand?"* — an appeal to their reason, not to their sentiment. Ibn Kathir unfolds the argument compressed inside it: "Someone has come calling you to what will benefit your situation in this life and the Hereafter without asking for any wage." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān runs the same reasoning from the other end: this is the second principle of the call — that he was a Messenger of Allah, that this call was the mission of his life, and that he was "working hard against heavy odds" to convey the message. Why would he? "If they thought about it, they would see that he was not asking them to pay for his services, nor did he receive any material benefits from them. If he did not honestly believe it to be the will and command of Allah, and right and true, why would he go to all that trouble of inviting them to believe and live a better life?"

The proof offered here is the man's own conduct — evidence a reasonable person can weigh.

## The prophetic mark: da'wah that costs the caller

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on this ayah to note a pattern across the whole Qur'an: **almost every prophet is reported saying that he asks for no payment** for the duty of *da'wah* (calling people to Allah). It draws a conclusion from that consistency — that where payment is accepted for da'wah and *tablīgh* (conveying the message), whether arranged in advance or simply expected by custom, "the call remains ineffective." And it adds the observation from lived experience: those who take wages for their religious sermons, addresses and counsels tend to "leave the hearts of their audience unchanged at the end of the exercise."

The point being made is about **effect on hearts**, and it cuts two ways for us. As listeners, we have a test: does the person calling you want something from you? As speakers — and every believer speaks to family and friends about Allah at some point — the weight of what we say is tied to how visibly free it is of self-interest.

## Ayah 52: forgiveness first, then turning back

"And O my people! Ask forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him."

Two commands, given in that order — and both commentaries distinguish them by the stretch of time each one covers.

- **Istighfār** (seeking forgiveness) faces **backwards**. Ibn Kathir: Hud, peace be upon him, "commanded them to seek the forgiveness of the One Who is capable of expiating previous sins." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies the content: forgiveness "for their disbelief and for sins they had committed in their past life."
- **Tawbah** (repentance, turning back) faces **forwards**. Ibn Kathir: "He also commanded them to repent for that which they may do in the future." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what that involves — that they "be ashamed of what they had done, repent and promise to themselves making a firm resolve and commitment that they would never go even near them."

So this is not one act said twice. It is a wiping clean of what is behind, then a decision about what is ahead. Regret without resolve leaves the road open; resolve without seeking forgiveness leaves the debt standing.

**What it opens up.** Ibn Kathir states the principle generally: "Whoever has these characteristics, Allah will make his sustenance easy for him, grant him ease in his affairs and guard over his situation." The ayah then names two gifts specifically:

**"He will send you abundant rain."** Ibn Kathir cites this phrase on its own, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it addressed a distress they were actually living through: the act of istighfār and tawbah "will remove the distress of famine from them. Heavy rains will come when due making their provisions sumptuous."

**"And add strength to your strength."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *quwwah* (strength, power) is used here "in a general sense which includes physical strength and power as well as the strength that comes from increases in wealth and children." Set that beside what we were told about 'Ad — a people known for their build, strength and bravery — and the offer touches the very thing they were proudest of: Allah offers to increase it, in return for the forgiveness and repentance they were being called to.

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a general lesson: tawbah and istighfār "have a special property of their own — that their practitioner is blessed with extended means of sustenance and satisfying increase in wealth and children, even in this mortal world." The everlasting prosperity of the Hereafter is beyond doubt; but the commentary insists that in this world too, the one who does this sincerely "will themselves notice its many benefits coming to them."

**"So do not turn away as criminals."** The ayah closes with the only other option. There is no neutral ground offered — either you take the two steps, or you turn your back, and the word the ayah chooses for those who turn their backs is "criminals." Having been shown the way out of both your sin and your drought, refusing it is itself the offence.

## Living it

- **Start where Hud, peace be upon him, started.** Before conduct, before ritual, the first question is whether anything shares the place in your heart that belongs to Allah alone. Whatever else you have set there, the Qur'an's verdict in ayah 50 is that you invented it.
- **Weigh a caller by what he wants from you.** Ayah 51 hands us a criterion that requires no scholarship to apply. And when we ourselves speak for Allah, the same criterion is turned on us.
- **Use istighfār and tawbah as more than words.** The order in ayah 52 gives a practical shape: name and seek forgiveness for what is past, then make a firm resolve about the future — not merely to stop, but as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, never to go near those things again.
- **Take the promise seriously when life is tight.** Both commentaries connect this pair of acts to relief in worldly matters — rain in a famine, ease in one's affairs, sustenance made easy, strength added to strength. When provision narrows or affairs tangle, the response prescribed to a people under famine is still available.

passages.title: 'Ad accuse Hūd; his defiant trust in Allah
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are one continuous exchange: 'Ad throw their rejection at Hud, peace be upon him (ayat 53–54), and Hud answers them (ayat 54–57). What holds the passage together is a single contrast — a people who have nothing but scorn and a slur to offer, and a lone man whose reply is not anger but a declaration of where his safety actually lies.

Read it as a scene. Hud stands before his people. They tell him their gods have driven him mad. He tells them to bring everything they have — themselves and their gods — and not to wait even a moment. That is not bravado. Ayah 56 explains exactly where such calm comes from.

## The charge: "you have brought us no proof" (ayah 53)

Their objection comes in three pieces, and Ibn Kathir separates them out.

First, **مَا جِئْتَنَا بِبَيِّنَةٍ** — "No evidence have you brought us." Ibn Kathir explains that they were claiming Hud "had not brought them any proof or evidence for what he claimed." Their charge is not that his message is unattractive; it is that, as they see it, nothing has been produced that obliges them to act.

Second, **وَمَا نَحْنُ بِتَارِكِي آلِهَتِنَا عَن قَوْلِكَ** — "and we shall not leave our gods for your (mere) saying!" Ibn Kathir puts their reasoning as a question they are throwing back at him: "how could his mere statement, 'Leave these gods,' be sufficient proof for them to leave their idols?" Notice what has happened to the burden of proof. They treat their inherited worship as the settled default, and treat the one calling them as the one who must argue his way in.

Third, **وَمَا نَحْنُ لَكَ بِمُؤْمِنِينَ** — "and we are not believers in you." Ibn Kathir's gloss is stark: "they did not believe what he was saying was true." This is the end of the argument, announced before any argument has been weighed. They are not asking for evidence; they are informing him that no evidence will be accepted.

## "Some of our gods have seized you with evil" (ayah 54)

Then comes the insult, and it is worth sitting with, because it tells you what these people actually believed. **إِن نَّقُولُ إِلَّا اعْتَرَاكَ بَعْضُ آلِهَتِنَا بِسُوءٍ** — "All that we say is that some of our gods have seized you with evil."

Ibn Kathir spells out what they meant: "We think that some of our idols have afflicted you with madness and insanity in your intellect because you are trying to stop them from being worshipped and defame them." In their picture of the world, the idols were agents who could be provoked and who could retaliate — and Hud's condition, as they diagnosed it, was the retaliation.

So there are two diagnoses on the table. Hud calls them away from their idols. They reply that his speech is not reasoning at all, it is an illness, and that their gods gave it to him. It is a move that has never gone out of use: when the argument cannot be answered, the arguer is declared unwell.

Note also how their two claims sit badly together. In ayah 53 they demand hard evidence before they will move an inch. In ayah 54 they are perfectly willing to assert, with nothing behind it, that objects of stone reached into a man's mind and unhinged it. The standard they impose on the truth is not the standard they apply to themselves.

## Hud's answer: a public disavowal (ayat 54–55)

He does not defend his sanity. He does something far more forceful. **قَالَ إِنِّي أُشْهِدُ اللَّهَ وَاشْهَدُوا أَنِّي بَرِيءٌ مِّمَّا تُشْرِكُونَ - مِن دُونِهِ** — "He said: 'I call Allah to witness and bear you witness, that I am free from that which you ascribe as partners in worship besides Him (Allah).'"

Ibn Kathir renders his meaning simply: "Verily, I am innocent of all of the rivals and idols (that you associate with Allah)."

Two details repay attention. The first is the double witnessing. He calls Allah to witness — and then he tells *them* to witness as well. He wants his disavowal on the record with the very people who oppose him. There is nothing private or hedged about his position; he is making sure that no one in that assembly can later claim they did not know where he stood.

The second is what he actually disowns: not belief in a Lord, but the partners ascribed in worship *besides Him*. Ibn Kathir's wording is "innocent of all of the rivals and idols." Hud is not saying "I disagree with your religion." He is saying he has no share in it and no connection to it at all.

## "So plot against me, all of you" (ayah 55)

**فَكِيدُونِي جَمِيعًا** — "So plot against me, all of you." Ibn Kathir explains who "all of you" includes: "you and your gods if they are true." That is the whole point. They had just accused his mind of being broken by their deities; he now invites those deities to finish the job, in public, with the entire nation joining in.

**ثُمَّ لَا تُنظِرُونِ** — "and give me no respite." Ibn Kathir supplies the measure Hud intends: not even "the blinking of an eye."

This is an argument disguised as a dare. Their entire case rested on the idols being potent enough to strike a man down. Hud stands in front of them, undefended, and asks for exactly that. Ibn Kathir draws out the conclusion explicitly: this argument of Hud's "contains a far-reaching proof and absolute evidence of the truthfulness of what Hud had come to them with. It also proves the falsehood of them worshipping idols that could not benefit nor harm them." Those idols, he says, "were inanimate objects that could not hear, see, befriend, or make enmity." A thing that cannot hear cannot be called upon, and a thing that cannot harm cannot be feared. The challenge is the proof.

## Where the courage comes from (ayah 56)

A man does not say "come at me, all of you" out of nothing. Ayah 56 gives the reason, and it is the heart of the whole passage.

**إِنِّي تَوَكَّلْتُ عَلَى اللَّهِ رَبِّي وَرَبِّكُم ۚ مَّا مِن دَابَّةٍ إِلَّا هُوَ آخِذٌ بِنَاصِيَتِهَا** — "I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord! There is not a moving creature but He has the grasp of its forelock."

Look at the phrase Hud chooses: "my Lord **and your Lord**." Even as he faces them down, he is still teaching. The One he relies on is not a private deity he happens to prefer; He is their Lord too, whether they acknowledge it or not. The very people who threaten him are under the authority of the One he is trusting.

And the ayah does not exempt anybody: *not one* moving creature. Not the chiefs of 'Ad. Not any crowd that might set upon Hud. Ibn Kathir's comment is exactly this: "Every creature is under His (Allah's) power and His authority."

Then the clause that keeps this from being merely a statement about raw power. Hud adds, "Verily, my Lord is on the straight path (the truth)," and Ibn Kathir explains: "He is the Best Judge, the Most Just, Who does not do any injustice in His ruling. For verily, He is upon the straight path."

Hud is not saying "my Lord is stronger than you, so watch out." He is saying that the One who holds every creature by the forelock is also perfectly just in how He rules. Total power in the hands of perfect justice — that is a thing a man can rest his life on. Ibn Kathir gathers up the force of Hud's whole argument: worship belongs to "Allah alone, without any partners. He is the One in Whose Hand is the sovereignty and He is in control of all things. There is nothing except that it is under His ownership, power and authority. Thus, there is no deity worthy of worship except Him and there is no Lord other than Him."

## The message is delivered; the outcome is not his to carry (ayah 57)

**فَإِن تَوَلَّوۡاْ فَقَدۡ أَبۡلَغۡتُكُم مَّآ أُرۡسِلۡتُ بِهِۦٓ إِلَيۡكُمۡ** — "So if you turn away, still I have conveyed the Message with which I was sent to you."

Ibn Kathir renders Hud's meaning: "If you turn away from that which I have brought to you in reference to worship of Allah, Who is your Lord alone, without any partners, then the proof has been established against you. This is because I have conveyed the Message of Allah to you, which He has sent me with."

That is the settling of accounts. They opened the exchange in ayah 53 by saying no proof had come. Hud closes it by stating that the proof has now been established against them — delivery is complete, and what they do with it is on their side of the ledger, not his. A messenger is charged with conveying, not with producing belief.

**وَيَسْتَخْلِفُ رَبِّي قَوْمًا غَيْرَكُمْ** — "My Lord will make another people succeed you, and you will not harm Him in the least."

Ibn Kathir explains that the successors are "a group of people who will worship Allah alone, without associating anything with Him," and that the statement "also implies that the polytheists do not bother Allah and they do not harm Him in the least with their disbelief. To the contrary, their disbelief merely harms their own selves."

Sit with that for a moment. They imagined they were doing damage — to Hud, to his message, even, in some vague way, to the claim he was making. In reality their rejection touched nothing but themselves. Allah is not diminished by being denied, and the worship of Allah on the earth does not stop because one nation refuses it; it simply passes to others.

**إِنَّ رَبِّي عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ حَفِيظٌ** — "Surely, my Lord is Guardian over all things." Ibn Kathir: "This means that Allah is a Witness and Guardian over the statements of His servants and their actions. He will give them due recompense for their actions. If they do good deeds, He will reward them with good. If they do evil, He will punish them with evil."

The exchange began with a demand for evidence and an accusation thrown at a man's mind. It ends with the reminder that there is a Witness and Guardian over the statements of every servant — including the accusation of madness in ayah 54 — and that nothing of it is lost or left unanswered.

## Living it

**Say clearly where you stand.** Hud's disavowal in ayat 54–55 was made out loud, in front of his opponents, with Allah called as witness and his opponents called as witnesses too. Faith that is never allowed to be visible has not yet been tested.

**Let the reliance come before the courage, not after.** The order in the passage matters: he issues the challenge in ayah 55, and ayah 56 tells us what he was standing on. Every creature that could threaten him was already in the grasp of the One he trusted. That is not a reason to be reckless; it is a reason not to be afraid of what has no power of its own.

**Do your part and release the result.** In ayah 57 Hud states plainly what he has done — he has conveyed what he was sent with. He does not measure himself by how many believed. If you carry the truth to family, colleagues, or your own children, the conveying is your work; the hearts are not.

**Take the slur without being knocked off course.** He was called mad in ayah 54 and never once argued about his sanity. He answered by pointing to Allah, and kept going.

**Remember who is actually harmed.** Rejection of the truth costs Allah nothing — Ibn Kathir is explicit that such disbelief "merely harms their own selves." That should drain the bitterness out of a believer's response to being refused, and replace it with concern for the one refusing.

passages.title: 'Ad destroyed and cursed in both worlds
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close the story of Hud and his people. Ayah 58 is the rescue, ayah 59 is the verdict read out against 'Ad, and ayah 60 is the sentence — a curse that follows them in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. What holds them together is a single moment: Allah's command arrives, and in that one instant the community splits in two. Some are lifted out by mercy; the rest are destroyed, and then named, charged, and condemned.

## "When Our command came" (58)

The story has been building to this. In ayah 57 Hud had finished his case: if you turn away, I have already conveyed the Message I was sent with, my Lord will make another people succeed you, you will not harm Him in the least, and *my Lord is Guardian over all things*. Then ayah 58 opens with **wa lammā jā'a amrunā** — "and when Our command came."

Ibn Kathir explains what that command was: **the barren wind with which Allah destroyed them, to the very last of them.** Nothing is described — no siege, no long decline. The Qur'an does not linger over the horror; it states the arrival of the command and moves straight to who was taken out of its path.

Notice how the rescue is stated. Ibn Kathir's rendering runs: *"We saved Hud and those who believed with him **by a mercy from Us**, and We saved them from a severe torment."* The saving is said twice — once with its cause, once with what they were saved from. And the cause is not their own strength or numbers. Ibn Kathir writes plainly: **the mercy and kindness of Allah, the Exalted, saved Hud and his followers from this terrible punishment.** They believed, yes — but the deliverance itself is credited to mercy. That is how the Qur'an teaches a believer to think about every rescue he has ever been given.

Note also who is saved: "Hud **and those who believed with him**." The ayah identifies them by their faith, not by anything else. And note what Hud had told them in ayah 57 — that Allah *"will make another people succeed you."* Ibn Kathir explains that this refers to **a group of people who will worship Allah alone, without associating anything with Him.**

## The verdict: "That was 'Ad" (59)

Ayah 59 shifts voice completely. Hud has stopped speaking; now Allah speaks *about* them, in the past tense, pointing back at them as a closed case: **wa tilka 'Ād** — "That was 'Ad," or as Ibn Kathir renders it, "Such were the people of 'Ad." They are no longer a living nation being warned. They are an exhibit.

Then comes the charge sheet, three counts:

**One: "They denied the signs of their Lord."** The verb is **jaḥadū**. Ibn Kathir's explanation is exact: **they disbelieved in the proofs and revelations of Allah.**

**Two: "and disobeyed His messengers."** Read that carefully. The one messenger they were dealing with was Hud, peace be upon him — yet the ayah says **rusulahu**, His messengers, in the plural. Ibn Kathir gives the reason, and it is one of the most important principles in the passage:

> **Whoever disbelieves in a Prophet, then verily, he has disbelieved in all of the Prophets, peace be upon them. There is no difference between any one of them, in the sense that it is necessary to believe in all of them. Therefore, 'Ad disbelieved in Hud, and their disbelief was considered disbelief in all of the Messengers.**

The prophets are not competing claims to be picked over. Believing in all of them is necessary; there is no difference between one and another in that respect. So rejecting the messenger standing in front of you is rejecting them all — which is why 'Ad, who rejected Hud, are charged with disobeying "messengers."

**Three: "and followed the command of every proud, obstinate one."** The Arabic is **jabbār 'anīd**. Ibn Kathir's rendering adds the gloss *oppressor of the truth from their leaders*, and he states the count against them exactly: **they abandoned following their rightly guided Messenger, and they followed the command of every proud, obstinate person.**

That is the trade at the heart of the passage. Everyone follows someone. 'Ad did not stop obeying — they moved their obedience from a rightly guided Messenger to proud, obstinate men. And note the word **every**: not one tyrant, but whichever one happened to be in front of them.

The ayah also keeps returning to one word: the signs of **their Lord**; they disbelieved in **their Lord**. This was not an argument with a stranger. Hud's whole call, as Ibn Kathir renders it, was to **the worship of Allah, Who is your Lord alone, without any partners** — and it is exactly that Lord they denied.

## The sentence: a curse in both worlds (60)

Ayah 60 uses a passive construction — **wa utbi'ū**, "and they were followed" or "pursued" — as though the curse were assigned to trail behind them. It follows them in **this world**, and it will follow them **on the Day of Resurrection**.

Ibn Kathir unpacks both halves. In this life, **they were followed by a curse from Allah and His believing servants whenever they are mentioned.** This is the strange afterlife of a destroyed nation: the wind finished them, but their name did not die — and Ibn Kathir ties the curse precisely to the mention of that name. Every time they are brought up, it follows them again.

And on the Day of Resurrection, Ibn Kathir says, **a call will be made against them in front of witnesses.** The verdict is not filed away quietly; it is called out, and there are witnesses to hear it.

Then the ayah seals it, in Ibn Kathir's rendering: **"No doubt! Verily, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. So away with 'Ad, the people of Hud."** Their final identity in the Book is fixed by the prophet they refused — *the people of Hud*.

## Reading it back to ayah 57

Two things Hud said just before this now land with full weight.

He said they **"will not harm Him in the least."** Ibn Kathir: **the polytheists do not bother Allah and they do not harm Him in the least with their disbelief; to the contrary, their disbelief merely harms their own selves.** Read ayat 58–60 and you see it demonstrated. 'Ad lost everything, in both worlds — and nothing was taken from Allah.

And he said: **"Surely, my Lord is Guardian (Ḥafīẓ) over all things."** Ibn Kathir explains: **Allah is a Witness and Guardian over the statements of His servants and their actions. He will give them due recompense for their actions. If they do good deeds, He will reward them with good. If they do evil, He will punish them with evil.** What that means here is that nothing was missed. The wind in ayah 58 was not a random disaster; it was the recompense for what had been witnessed and kept in full.

## Where the surah goes next

The pattern does not stop with 'Ad. Maarif ul Quran notes that the next eight ayat (61–68) carry the story of Salih, peace be upon him, **sent to the people of Thamud, another branch of the tribe of 'Ad** — another prophet inviting his people to *tawḥīd*, the Oneness of Allah, another refusal, and, in the end, the rescue of the prophet and his companions while the rest were destroyed. The same shape as ayat 58–60, laid down again. That repetition is itself part of what surah Hud is teaching.

## Living it

**Judge your obedience, not your opinions.** 'Ad's ruin is described as a change of leadership: they abandoned following their rightly guided Messenger and followed "every proud, obstinate one." Ask honestly who is actually shaping your choices — whose approval you are chasing, whose voice you cannot bear to contradict. Nobody follows nobody.

**Believe in all the messengers.** The principle Ibn Kathir draws here is not decorative: whoever disbelieves in one Prophet has disbelieved in all of them, because believing in all of them is necessary and there is no difference between them in that.

**Never take your rescue as a wage you earned.** Hud and the believers were saved *by a mercy from Us* — Ibn Kathir calls it the mercy and kindness of Allah. When you come out of something intact, the correct response is gratitude to the One who is Ḥafīẓ over all things, not self-congratulation.

**Take the warning while the door is open.** Ayah 58 begins *when Our command came* — and by then the case had already been closed. Hud's entire argument belonged to the time before. So does ours.

passages.title: Ṣāliḥ, the she-camel, and three days' respite
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath.** These five ayat carry a single scene from beginning to end: Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) is sent to the people of Thamūd and calls them to worship Allah alone; they answer him with an appeal to his old reputation, to ancestral custom, and to declared doubt; he places a sign before them — the she-camel — and when they kill her, the arguing stops and a countdown starts. What holds the passage together is that one movement: **invitation (61) → rejection (62) → the messenger's reply (63) → the sign and its single condition (64) → the crime and the three days (65).**

## Who Thamūd were

Ibn Kathir describes them as a people "living in cities carved from the rocks, between Tabuk and Al-Madinah" in Arabia, and adds that "they lived after the people of 'Ad." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says Thamūd were "another branch of the tribe of ʿĀd" — so this is a later people of the same stock.

One detail of that description matters for reading ayah 61: these were not a wandering people. They were builders, settled enough to have cities cut into the rock itself.

Ayah 61 introduces the messenger as **"their brother Ṣāliḥ"** — that is the Qur'an's own word for him, and it is worth holding on to as their answer unfolds.

## The call itself (61)

Ṣāliḥ's opening, in Ibn Kathir's summary, is one thing: "He commanded them to worship Allah alone." Everything else in the ayah supports that one command — "O my people! Worship Allah: you have no other god but Him."

**"He brought you forth from the earth."** Ibn Kathir explains: "He began your creation from it (the earth). From it He created your father, Adam." The argument is an argument from origin — before you owned anything, you *were* nothing but earth, and Someone raised you out of it.

**"and settled you therein."** Ibn Kathir's gloss on *wa-staʿmarakum fīhā* is: "He made you prosperous in the earth. You are settled in it and you treasure it." Notice how precisely that lands on a people whose cities were carved from the rocks. The settlement, the prosperity, the treasuring of the place — all of it is named back to them as a gift. The One who raised you from the dust is the One who then made you comfortable in it.

**"then ask forgiveness of Him and turn to Him in repentance."** Ibn Kathir draws a fine and very useful distinction between the two commands:

- *fa-staghfirūhu* (ask forgiveness) — "this is in reference to your previous sins"
- *thumma tūbū ilayhi* (turn to Him in repentance) — "this is in reference to the future"

So it is not one idea said twice. *Istighfār* settles the account behind you; *tawbah* is the turn of the face forward, a commitment about the life still ahead. A man may ask pardon for what he did last night and still be walking in the same direction this morning; ayah 61 asks for both — the pardon and the turn.

**"Certainly, my Lord is Near, Responsive."** This is where the call stops being a demand and becomes an invitation. Ibn Kathir renders it "Near (to all by His knowledge), Responsive," and pairs it with Allah's statement in Sūrah al-Baqarah:

> And when My servants ask you concerning Me, then (answer them), I am indeed Near (to them by My knowledge). I respond to the invocations of the supplicant when he calls on Me. *(2:186)*

The parentheses are Ibn Kathir's own, and they carry the point: the nearness he is describing is a nearness of knowledge, and it comes paired with response. Nothing you say is outside His knowing, and the supplicant who calls on Him is answered. That is the Lord Ṣāliḥ is calling a people of idols towards — One who is Near, and who replies.

## The backstory ayah 64 assumes

If you read ayah 64 straight after ayah 63, the she-camel appears from nowhere: "This she-camel of Allah is a sign for you." The Qur'an does not narrate her arrival here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what the passage takes as known:

> As customary, his people belied him and insisted that he must first make a she-camel of a specified description come out from the rock of the mountain in front of them in order to have them believe that he was a true prophet of Allah.

Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) warned them before it happened, and the warning shapes everything that follows. Maʿārif reports him saying that **if Allah shows them the very miracle they had custom-ordered and they still fail to believe, then according to the customary practice of Allah the punishment will come and destroy all of them.** They remained obstinate. And Maʿārif continues: "The rock of the mountain in front of them split asunder. Out from it came the she-camel bearing the features specified by them."

This is worth pausing on. They did not receive a sign of Allah's choosing — they received *their own specification*, delivered to order, in front of their eyes. Maʿārif then records the single condition: "Allah Ta'ala ordered them not to harm that she-camel in any manner, otherwise the punishment will come upon them."

## "You were our great hope" (62)

Their reply opens not with an argument but with an appeal to his standing among them: *"O Ṣāliḥ! You have been among us as a figure of good hope until this!"* Ibn Kathir introduces the whole reply plainly — Allah "informs of their ignorance and obstinacy in their statement" — and glosses their words as: "We had hope in your strong intellect before you began saying what you have said."

That last clause is the hinge. Their complaint is dated. It is not that he became untrustworthy; it is that he began saying what he said.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens this up. Before he claimed prophethood and told them to shun idol-worship, they had great hopes in him; they thought he would rise to be a great reformer and leader of their people. And the reason, Maʿārif explains, is that **Allah nurtures and grooms His prophets from their childhood in a way that they become models of good morals and habits — whoever looks at them loves and respects them.**

Maʿārif then draws the parallel with the Prophet ﷺ:

> Before he declared that he has been sent as a prophet, the whole Arabia called him al-amin (the trustworthy one) and took him to be true and righteous. It was only when he announced his prophet-hood and prohibited idol-worship that everyone turned hostile to him.

Read that back into the sūrah and the pattern is the same in both cases: the same man, the same character, widely admired — until he named their idols. What changed was not the messenger. It was the message.

**"Do you now forbid us the worship of what our fathers worshipped?"** Ibn Kathir glosses this as "what those who were before us were upon." This is the second move: when reputation fails, appeal to inheritance. Notice that they never claim their idols are true — only that they are ancestral. Custom is offered where evidence should be.

**"But we are really in grave doubt as to that to which you invite us."** Ibn Kathir comments that this "alludes to the great amount of doubt that they had." Set that beside how he framed the whole speech — ignorance and obstinacy — and note where the doubt sits in the conversation: it arrives *after* the appeal to reputation and *after* the appeal to the fathers, as the last of three answers, none of which is an argument about the truth of what he said.

## Ṣāliḥ's answer (63)

His reply does not defend himself and does not attack their idols. It re-frames the whole question — *"Tell me / consider: if I have a clear proof from my Lord, and there has come to me a mercy from Him…"*

**"a clear proof from my Lord."** On *bayyinah*, Ibn Kathir has Ṣāliḥ saying: "In reference to what He (Allah) has sent me with to you, I am upon conviction and sure evidence." Against their "grave doubt" he sets *conviction*. That is the axis of the exchange: their uncertainty is a state of mind; his certainty rests on what his Lord sent him with.

**"who then can help me against Allah, if I were to disobey Him?"** Ibn Kathir explains precisely what the disobedience in question would be: that Ṣāliḥ should "abandon calling you to the truth and the worship of Allah alone." In other words — *you are asking me to stop. Suppose I did. Who then rescues me from Allah?* The question relocates the risk. The danger being weighed is not their displeasure; it is Allah's.

**"Then you increase me not but in loss."** Ibn Kathir continues the sense: if he did abandon the call, "you would not be able to bring me any benefit, nor increase me… but in loss" — and on *ghayra takhsīr* he says simply, "This means loss and ruin." Everything they hold out to him — their approval, the leadership they had once hoped he would take up — is, on that reckoning, not profit but pure subtraction.

## The she-camel and the single command (64)

*"And O my people! This she-camel of Allah is a sign for you. So leave her to graze in Allah's land, and touch her not with evil, lest a near torment should seize you."*

Look at how little is asked. She is *nāqat Allāh* — the she-camel *of Allah* — and she grazes in *Allah's land*: in the ayah's own words, both she and the pasture are ascribed to Him. And the command is not "feed her", not "tend her", not "honour her with ritual". It is *fa-dharūhā* — **leave her to graze.** Her food is already provided on Allah's earth. All that is required of Thamūd is that they do not interfere.

That is what makes the crime so bare. The one condition attached to the sign they had themselves specified was that they keep their hands off it.

**"lest a near torment should seize you."** Hold on to the word *near*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān returns to this exact phrase when the punishment arrives, and reads it as the warning that was fulfilled.

## Three days (65)

*"But they slaughtered her."* One clause — *fa-ʿaqarūhā* — and the argument is over. The Qur'an spends no words here on how or why.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out what followed: "when these people killed the she-camel associated with the miracle in flagrant contravention of the Divine command, then, something serious happened. As warned earlier, 'lest a near punishment should seize you - 64', the punishment did come upon them in a manner that they were given a respite of three days and told that they all will be destroyed on the fourth day."

**"Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days."** The word *tamattaʿū* — take your enjoyment — is bitter here. Their prosperity, the very *staʿmarakum* of ayah 61, is handed back to them for three days. Everything they cut out of the rock becomes simply a place to wait.

**"This is a promise (a threat) that will not be belied."** Ibn Kathir's parenthesis names what kind of promise it is. The three days are not an escape clause; Ṣāliḥ tells them plainly that the appointment will be kept, and there is no confusion left about what is coming or why.

Ibn Kathir closes his comment on this passage by noting that a discussion of this story "has already preceded in Surat Al-A'raf and it is sufficient without having to be repeated here" — a useful pointer if you want the story at greater length.

## Living it

**Two motions, not one.** Ayah 61 asks for *istighfār* for what is behind and *tawbah* for what is ahead. Make both habits: seek pardon for the specific thing, then decide the specific change. Ibn Kathir's small distinction is a whole method of repentance.

**Prosperity is a gift with a name on it.** Thamūd were told, in the middle of their achievement, that the earth they had mastered was the same earth they were made from, and that He "made you prosperous in the earth." Success does not create independence from Allah; it usually just hides the dependence better.

**Notice which of your objections are actually arguments.** Thamūd's three answers were his old reputation, their fathers' practice, and their own doubt — and Ibn Kathir names the whole reply as ignorance and obstinacy. It is worth asking of our own hesitations whether they engage the claim at all.

**"Our fathers did it" is not evidence.** Ayah 62 records the argument from inheritance without dignifying it with a reply. Inherited practice is worth examining; it was never worth worshipping.

**Expect the reputation to go.** Maʿārif's parallel with the Prophet ﷺ, whom the whole of Arabia called *al-amin* until he prohibited idol-worship, is a caution for anyone who calls to the truth: approval that depends on your silence was never approval of you.

**Ask Ṣāliḥ's question.** *"Who then can help me against Allah, if I were to disobey Him?"* When pressure comes to soften what you know to be true, that single question — put to yourself — settles most of it.

**He is Near, and He answers.** For all the severity of this passage, the sentence at its head is an open door: *"Certainly, my Lord is Near, Responsive."* That was the invitation Thamūd were given, and ayah 65 is what came of refusing it.

passages.title: The blast that erased Thamūd
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the fourth day. In ayah 65, after Thamūd had slaughtered the she-camel that Allah had made a sign for them, Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) told them: *"Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. This is a promise (a threat) that will not be belied."* Ayat 66–68 are what happened when those three days ran out — a rescue, a sound, and an erasure. What holds the passage together is a single hinge: one community, one appointed day, two completely different endings.

## The countdown that was honoured to the day

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the sequence. When these people killed the she-camel associated with the miracle, in flagrant contravention of the divine command, the warning of ayah 64 — *"lest a near torment should seize you"* — came due. But it came in a particular way: they were given a respite of three days and told that they would all be destroyed on the fourth day.

Citing Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that those three days were Thursday, Friday and Saturday, and that on Sunday the punishment descended upon them.

Notice what that means. This was not a sudden strike. It was an announced, dated appointment — and they lived inside it for three days, knowing the day that was coming. The wording of ayah 65 is almost tender in its bitterness: *enjoy yourselves in your homes*. Homes are where safety lives. Three days later those same homes are where their bodies are found (ayah 67). The phrase "a promise that will not be belied" is the point on which the whole passage turns: when Allah announces a term, nothing in creation delays it or brings it forward.

## Ayah 66: rescue before ruin

*"So when Our commandment came, We saved Ṣāliḥ and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that Day. Verily, your Lord — He is the All-Strong, the All-Mighty."*

Three things in this ayah repay slow reading.

**"When Our commandment came."** The command is spoken of as something that *comes* — it reaches its appointed hour and arrives. Everything before this — the sign, the warning, the three days — was the waiting room of a decision already made.

**"We saved… by a mercy from Us."** The salvation is immediately traced to its source. The believers are not credited with saving themselves. Their faith is what distinguished them, but their rescue is attributed here to Allah's mercy.

**"And from the disgrace of that Day."** Ṣāliḥ and the believers were delivered from two things, not one: from the punishment itself, and from the disgrace of that Day. They were not merely kept alive; they were kept out of the humiliation. A person can survive a catastrophe and still be covered in its shame. These were spared both.

**"Verily, your Lord — He is the All-Strong, the All-Mighty."** The ayah closes by naming Allah as the All-Strong and the All-Mighty. Placed here, those words answer the obvious question the story raises: how did a whole people who felt untouchable end up as bodies in their houses? Because the Lord who warned them is the All-Strong, and no strength stands against His.

Note too the possessive: *your* Lord. The address turns toward the one hearing it. The story is not being told merely as history; it is told to a listener, about the Lord who is his own.

## Ayah 67: the Cry

*"And As-Sayhah (awful cry) overtook the wrongdoers, so they lay (dead), prostrate in their homes."*

**The Cry.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this awesome Cry was that of the archangel Jibrīl (peace be upon him) — far more terrifying, it says, than the combined thunderbolts of worldly lightning could ever be, something human senses could not take. All hearts were rent apart by the horrific sound, and those people were destroyed in a mass.

Sit with the mechanism for a moment. No army. No siege. No weapon a confident, well-established people could have prepared against. A sound. What ended Thamūd had no substance to it at all, because when Allah decrees a thing there is no need for machinery.

**"The wrongdoers."** The ayah does not say "the Cry seized Thamūd." It says it overtook *the wrongdoers* — those who wronged. The punishment is attached to the description, not merely to the tribe's name. Wrongdoing is what made them liable, and wrongdoing is what the sound came for. Ṣāliḥ and those who believed with him were of the very same people; what separated them was that they were not among the wrongdoers.

**"So they lay (dead), prostrate in their homes."** The settlement that had been alive lay dead in the very houses they had been told to enjoy for three days. The place of safety became the place where they were found.

## The Cry and the earthquake

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises an honest question here, and it is worth learning from how it is handled.

From this ayah we learn that the people of Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) were destroyed by a severe Sound. But Sūrat al-Aʿrāf says of them, *"So, the earthquake seized them"* (7:78, 91) — which, as is obvious, tells us the punishment visiting them was that of the earthquake. Two different agents of destruction, for one event.

Al-Qurṭubī, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, said that there is no contradiction here. It is possible that the earthquake came first and then they were all destroyed by the severe Sound. And the discussion closes with the words that should close every such discussion: *Allah knows best.*

Two lessons sit inside that small paragraph. First, the method: when two Qur'anic passages describe the same event differently, the default of the scholars is not to pit them against each other but to look for the reading in which both are true — here, simply a sequence of events rather than rival accounts. Second, the manners: al-Qurṭubī offers the reconciliation as a possibility ("it is possible"), not as a fact he can prove, and then hands the matter back to Allah. Confidence about the text; humility about our reconstruction of the details.

## Ayah 68: as if they had never lived there

*"As if they had never lived there. No doubt! Verily, Thamūd disbelieved in their Lord. So away with Thamūd!"*

**"As if they had never lived there."** This is the harshest sentence in the passage and the most instructive. It is not enough that they died; the record of their having been there is spoken of as if wiped. A people with homes and a name — and the Qur'an describes the aftermath as though the ground had never known them.

**"No doubt! Verily, Thamūd disbelieved in their Lord."** The passage names the cause so that no one can misread the story. Not: they were unlucky. Not: something in the world happened to go against them. *They disbelieved in their Lord* — and note the relationship the words insist on. It was not some distant deity they rejected; it was **their** Lord, the One who sent them a prophet who called them "my people," gave them a plain sign in the she-camel, warned them of a near torment, and then still gave them three days.

**"So away with Thamūd!"** The last words are not a description but a pronouncement — a sentence of dismissal, of being cast far off. It is the closing verdict on the file. And the "No doubt!" that opens the sentence before it is the Qur'an's way of taking the listener by the collar: do not let this one pass you by.

## A note on how Ibn Kathir handles this

Ibn Kathir's own commentary on these ayat is remarkably brief. He quotes the passage in full and then simply says that a discussion of this story has already preceded in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf and that it is sufficient without having to be repeated here — closing with, "Allah is the Giver of success."

That restraint is itself instructive. Rather than repeat himself, he points the reader to where the fuller treatment already sits. It is also a quiet reminder for the reader: the story of Thamūd is told in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf as well — the same sūrah Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns to over the earthquake — and the fuller picture comes from reading the accounts together rather than expecting one passage to carry everything.

## Living it

**Respite is not the same as safety.** Thamūd had three days in which nothing at all happened. Nothing happening is not evidence that nothing is coming. Delay, in the Qur'an's account of them, was room given — not a verdict cancelled.

**What separated the two groups was faith, and what saved them was mercy.** Ayah 66 is precise: those who believed were saved *by a mercy from Us*. Belief is what put them on the right side of the line; mercy is what carried them across it. Both halves of that sentence protect the heart — the first from complacency, the second from self-congratulation.

**The punishment came for a description, not a label.** Ayah 67 overtakes *the wrongdoers*. Sharing a name, a lineage, a town or a community with the righteous saved nobody. Each person's standing was their own.

**Permanence is an illusion.** Ayah 68's "as if they had never lived there" is aimed squarely at whoever assumes their own arrangements are too solid to disappear.

**Read the ending as an address, not an anecdote.** *"Verily, your Lord — He is the All-Strong, the All-Mighty."* The sentence is not left in the past tense with Thamūd; it is turned toward whoever is listening. Whatever strength seems to be arrayed against the truth, the Lord being described is the All-Strong and the All-Mighty — and the outcome was never in the hands of those who dismiss you.

passages.title: Abraham's guests and the news of Isaac
passages.tafsir:
**In one glance.** Ayat 69–73 tell of a single visit: angels in human form arrive at the house of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), he hurries to feed them, they will not touch the food, fear stirs in him — and then the visit opens out into two errands at once. They carry good news of a son and a grandson to a couple long past childbearing, and they are on their way to the people of Lut. Ibn Kathir titles the passage "The Coming of the Angels to Ibrahim and Their Glad Tidings to Him of Ishaq and Ya'qub." What binds the five ayat together is that one delegation, carrying mercy in one hand and punishment in the other.

## Who the "messengers" are, and what the "good news" was

Ayah 69 opens: *"And verily, there came Our messengers to Ibrahim with the glad tidings."* Ibn Kathir notes plainly that **"messengers" here means angels**, not human prophets. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, citing al-Qurtubi, that the three angels were Jibra'il, Mika'il and Israfil. Ibn Kathir separately cites As-Suddi, who said that when Allah sent the angels to the people of Lut, "they set out walking in the form of young men."

Maʿārif sets the scene: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had no children from his wife Sarah and wished for them, but the two of them were much advanced in years — so, humanly speaking, there was no hope.

What was *al-bushrā*, "the glad tidings"? Ibn Kathir records two views among the commentators: that it means "Receive the glad tidings of Ishaq," and that it means the destruction of the people of Lut. He judges the first to be correct, and his proof is a later ayah in this surah: *"Then when the fear had gone away from Ibrahim, and the glad tidings had reached him, he began to plead with Us for the people of Lut"* (11:74). Maʿārif makes the same structural observation from another angle: ayah 69 tells us the angels came with good news, and the content of that news is only given later, in ayah 71 — *"so We gave her the good news about Ishaq."*

## "They said: Salaman. He answered: Salamun."

The angels greeted with *salāman*; Ibrahim answered with *salāmun*. In English both come out as "peace," but Ibn Kathir reports that **the scholars of explanation said Ibrahim's reply was better than the greeting he received** — and the difference is a single vowel at the end of the word.

The reason they gave is that the second form, *salāmun*, stands in what they call the subjective case, and this "alludes to affirmation and eternity." Ibrahim did not merely return a greeting; the form of his words carried something settled and lasting. He received courtesy and returned something better.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical lesson: this is the Sunnah of *salām* between Muslims — **the guest coming in should say it first, and those present should respond**. And it points out that the word *salām* here stands as shorthand for the full greeting; the complete form taught to this community by the Prophet ﷺ in word and deed is *As-salāmu ʿalaykum* at the beginning, and *wa ʿalaykumu-s-salām* — or, to be more generous, *wa ʿalaykumu-s-salāmu wa raḥmatullāh* — in reply. Maʿārif observes what is lost when we flatten this into "peace on you": every community has some greeting when people meet, but this one **carries the name of Allah in it**, so it is at once a *dhikr* (remembrance) of Allah, a prayer to Him for the other person's peace and protection, and a guarantee from the speaker's own side of the protection of that person's life, property and honour.

## The calf brought without delay

*"And he hastened to entertain them with a roasted calf."* Ibn Kathir reads the phrase as motion: Ibrahim **left with haste** to bring them food, as a host does. The word for how it was cooked, *ḥanīdh*, means roasted upon heated stones — a meaning reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and others. He connects this with the parallel telling in Surat adh-Dhāriyāt: *"Then he turned to his household, and brought out a roasted calf. And placed it before them, saying: Will you not eat?"* (51:26–27) — and comments that this verse contains **many aspects of the etiquettes of hosting guests**.

Maʿārif, drawing on al-Qurtubi, fills in the portrait. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is the first human being who introduced the custom of honouring guests by offering them hospitality; it was his routine that **he would never eat alone** — when mealtime came he would be looking out for a guest so that he could eat with him.

Al-Qurtubi also relates, from Isra'ili narratives, that one day Ibrahim went looking for a guest at mealtime and the man he met was a stranger. When the man sat down to eat, Ibrahim said to him, "Say: I begin with the name of Allah." The man replied, "I do not know Allah. Who and what is He?" — and Ibrahim asked him to leave the food-spread. When he had gone, Jibra'il came in and said: Allah says, *As for him, We gave sustenance to him throughout his life despite his disbelief; and as for you, you were stingy about giving him even one morsel of food.* Hearing this, Ibrahim went after the man and called him back. The man said he would not come unless he was told why he had been turned out first and why he was now being asked back in. When Ibrahim told him the whole episode, the episode itself became the reason for the man's becoming a believer. He said, "The Lord who made you do this is very noble. I believe in Him," and he went back in, behaved like a true believer, and ate his food after having recited *Bismillah* first.

From ayah 69 Maʿārif derives three rules of hospitality, following al-Qurtubi:

1. **Bring something out quickly.** It is part of the etiquette of hospitality that soon after the guest arrives the host brings out something to eat or drink that he has on hand and can offer quickly and conveniently. Then, if he is a man of means, he can arrange for additional hospitality later.
2. **Do not fuss over formality.** A host should not worry about making too many formal arrangements. Anything good that is easily available is good enough. Ibrahim had some domestic animals at home, so he slaughtered a calf, had it roasted quickly, and offered it to his guests.
3. **Hospitality is a hallmark of high morals** — part of the essential etiquette of Islam and the blessed habit of the prophets and the righteous. Is it obligatory (*wājib*)? Here the scholars genuinely differ. According to the majority it is *sunnah* and desirable, but not *wājib*. Some say it is *wājib* upon village people to offer hospitality to a person staying in their village, because a stranger there has no arrangement for his meals, whereas in cities such arrangements are possible through a hotel, so it is not *wājib* on city dwellers. Al-Qurtubi reports all these different views in his Tafsir.

## The price of the meal

Two separate narrations of what passed at the table come down to us, and they are worth keeping distinct.

**As-Suddi's account, as Ibn Kathir cites it:** Ibrahim slaughtered the calf, roasted it on hot stones, brought it to them and sat down with them, and when he placed it before them said, "Will you not eat?" They said, "O Ibrahim! Verily, we do not eat food without a price." Ibrahim said, "Verily, this food has a price." They said, "What is its price?" He said: **"You must mention the Name of Allah over it before eating it and praise Allah upon finishing it."** Jibril then looked at Mika'il and said, "This man has the right that his Lord should take him as an intimate friend."

**Al-Tabari's report, as Maʿārif relates it at this place:** when the angels first abstained from eating, they said that they do not eat free meals — if they were to accept payment for it, they would. Ibrahim said, "Yes, there is a price for it that you can pay. The price is: say 'with the name of Allah' when you begin, and praise Him when you finish." Hearing this, Jibra'il told his companions, "That Allah calls him His friend is correct. He deserves it."

Maʿārif draws the ruling out of it: saying **Bismillāh** when beginning to eat and **Alḥamdulillāh** at the end of it is Sunnah. And notice what Ibrahim asked for as payment — not wealth, but that Allah be named at his table.

## Fear in the heart of a prophet

Ayah 70: *"But when he saw their hands went not towards it, he mistrusted them, and conceived a fear of them."* Ibn Kathir explains *nakirahum* as **he felt estranged from them**. And the fear? Because **angels are not concerned with food** — they do not desire it, nor do they eat it. So when Ibrahim saw them reject the food he had brought without tasting any of it at all, he felt a mistrust of them.

Maʿārif adds two things that make the moment human. First, why did the angels not simply eat? They had come in human form, and it was possible that they could have been given the human characteristics of eating and drinking at that time; but the wiser choice was that they should *not* eat, so that the secret of their being angels would come out into the open. Their angelic characteristics were allowed to remain even inside the human form, which is why their hands did not go towards the food. Second, according to some reports they had arrows in their hands and started poking the heads of their arrows into the roasted meat. When they acted in that way Ibrahim took them to be enemies, because **by the social custom known to him, a guest refusing to eat was a sign of mischief to be made from his side** (al-Qurtubi).

His apprehension was quashed the moment the angels disclosed who they were. Ibn Kathir renders their reassurance: *"Do not be afraid of us. Verily, we are angels sent to the people of Lut in order to destroy them."* Maʿārif adds that they told him there was no danger for him to bother about.

## Sarah standing, and her laugh

Ayah 71: *"And his wife was standing there, and she laughed."* Maʿārif explains the scene — Sarah was listening to the conversation from behind a curtain, and when she found out that they were angels and not human beings, the *hijab* that would otherwise have been essential was not needed.

Why did she laugh? The sources give more than one reading, and both are worth holding. In As-Suddi's account cited by Ibn Kathir, when Sarah looked and saw that her husband was honouring these guests she began to serve them, laughing, and said, *"What amazing guests we have. We serve them ourselves, showing them respect, and they do not eat our food."* Then, when the angels disclosed their mission, Ibn Kathir says **she laughed in delight at the good news of the destruction of Lut's people** — because they had caused much corruption and their disbelief was severe. And, he adds, **for this reason she was rewarded** with the glad tidings of a son, even after her despair. Maʿārif reads her laugh as the response to the good news of the birth of a child in old age. Either way, the sequence in the ayah is exact: she laughs, and immediately — *"But We gave her glad tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, of Ya'qub."*

## Two generations promised in one breath

The gift is doubled before it is given. Not only a son, but *"and after Ishaq, of Ya'qub"* — Ibn Kathir explains this as the grandson: the son she was going to have would himself have a son who would succeed him and beget many children. For Ya'qub was the son of Ishaq, just as Allah says: *"Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub, when he said unto his sons: What will you worship after me? They said: We shall worship your Deity (ilāh), the Deity of your fathers Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq, One Deity, and to Him we submit"* (2:133). For a woman who had already despaired, this is not merely "a child" — it is a line, a future, a household.

Ibn Kathir also builds a serious argument on this half-verse. Because the glad tidings included a son named Ya'qub to be born to Ishaq, **Ishaq could not have been the son whom Ibrahim was commanded to sacrifice**: how could Ibrahim be commanded to sacrifice him while he was still a small child and no son named Ya'qub had yet been born to him, when that son had been promised — and the promise of Allah is true, and there is no breaking of Allah's promise? Ibn Kathir concludes that Isma'il was the son who was to be sacrificed, and calls this "the best, most correct and clearest evidence of that."

## "Woe unto me! Shall I bear a child?"

Ayah 72: *"She said, in astonishment: Woe unto me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman, and here is my husband an old man? Verily, this is a strange thing!"*

Ibn Kathir sets her words beside her gesture. Allah speaks of her statement in this verse, just as He speaks of her action in another: *"Then his wife came forward with a loud voice: she smote her face, and said: A barren old woman!"* (51:29). And he explains: **this was the custom of the women in their speech and actions when they were expressing amazement.** Here the Qur'an reports what she said; there it reports what she did. The Qur'an is unembarrassed to record the exact reaction of a real person to news like this.

## "Do you wonder at the decree of Allah?"

Ayah 73 is the answer, and it is the heart of the passage. Ibn Kathir unfolds the angels' words: *do not be amazed at the command of Allah, for whenever He wants something He merely says "Be" and it is. So do not be amazed at this, even though you are old and barren and your husband is a very old man. Verily, Allah is able to do whatever He wills.*

Maʿārif adds a second layer to the gentle rebuke: as a member of the prophet's family, had she not been witnessing that this was a family upon which **extraordinary Divine mercy and blessing descends all the time, mostly above and beyond the obvious chain of causes**? So what was there to wonder about? And that is exactly what the angels say next: *"The mercy of Allah and His blessings be on you, O the family of Ibrahim."* The astonishment is answered with a blessing.

**"Surely, He is All-Praiseworthy, All-Glorious"** — *Ḥamīd, Majīd*. Ibn Kathir explains: this means that He is the Most Praiseworthy in all of His actions and statements; He is praised and glorified in His Attributes and His Self.

## From the Sunnah

It is at this point, and for this reason — the two names that close the ayah — that Ibn Kathir brings the hadith he describes as **confirmed in the two Ṣaḥīḥs**, in which the Companions said, "Verily, we already know how to greet you with *salām*, but how do we send *ṣalāh* upon you, O Messenger of Allah?" He ﷺ said:

> *"Say: O Allah, send prayers upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, just as You have sent prayers upon Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, just as You have blessed the family of Ibrahim. Truly, You are the All-Praiseworthy, All-Glorious."*

Read the two texts side by side and the link Ibn Kathir is making is plain: the angels' words at Ibrahim's table ask mercy and blessing upon the family of Ibrahim and close with *Ḥamīd, Majīd*; the prayer the Prophet ﷺ taught asks blessing upon Muhammad and his family as it was given to the family of Ibrahim, and closes with the same two names.

## Living it

The passage is unusually practical. From it the scholars draw:

- **Greet first, and answer better.** The one arriving gives *salām*; those present respond — and Ibrahim's reply teaches that the answer can be better than the greeting received.
- **Feed people, and do it fast.** Bring out what you have without delay and without fuss. Hospitality is the habit of the prophets and the righteous, a hallmark of high morals.
- **Guests have manners too.** Maʿārif takes from *"their hands went not towards it"* that a guest should accept whatever is offered and partake of it a little to please the host, even if he is unwilling to eat because of an unfavourable taste.
- **Watch, but do not stare.** The host should not consider himself absolved once the food is placed down; he should benignly notice whether the guest is eating, as Ibrahim did. But the watching must be discreet — a casual look is enough, because looking at the morsels a guest is eating is contrary to the etiquette of entertainment and humiliating for him. Maʿārif illustrates this with the Caliph Hisham ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, who was sharing his food-spread with a rustic Arab and pointed out a strand of hair in the man's morsel; the Arab rose at once in a huff and said, "We never eat with a person who watches our morsels."
- **Name Allah over your food.** *Bismillāh* at the start, *Alḥamdulillāh* at the end — the price Ibrahim asked of his guests, and, as Maʿārif concludes, a Sunnah.
- **Do not measure the decree of Allah by the causes you can see.** Sarah was old and barren and her husband a very old man — and the angels told her not to be amazed: when Allah wants something He merely says *"Be"* and it is, and He is able to do whatever He wills.

passages.title: Abraham pleads for Lot's people
passages.tafsir:
**These three ayat are one scene.** A fright has passed. Glad tidings have arrived. And in that same moment Ibrahim (peace be upon him) turns and pleads for a people already marked for destruction — until he is told, by name, to stop. What binds ayat 74–76 together is a single movement: relief, then intercession, then a divine halt that arrives wrapped in praise rather than rebuke.

## What "the fear had left him" refers to

Ibn Kathir renders ayah 74 this way: *"Then when the fear had gone away from (the mind of) Ibrahim, and the glad tidings had reached him, he began to plead with Us (Our messengers) for the people of Lut."*

Two words in the Arabic carry the setup. The first, **al-rawʿ**, is given as "fear" in the translation before us and as "fright" by Ibn Kathir. The second, **al-bushrā**, is "the good news" in the translation and "the glad tidings" in Ibn Kathir.

What was the fright, and what was the news? Ibn Kathir answers both. Allah "informs of what happened after the fright of Ibrahim left him and he felt no more fear of the angels **when they refused to eat**." Their refusal is what settled him. And the glad tidings, he notes, were of two things at once: **the birth of a son, and the destruction of the people of Lut**.

The order of the ayah is deliberate. Only after the fear had gone, and only after the good news had reached him, did Ibrahim begin to plead. The pleading was not a reaction of panic. It came from a man whose fear had lifted and whose news was good — and he spent that moment arguing for someone else.

## Who he was pleading for

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the setting. Allah sent angels, Jibril (peace be upon him) among them, "to execute the punishment against these people." They came first to Ibrahim in Palestine, and afterwards "they came to Sayyidna Lut whose abode was located at a distance of ten or twelve miles from there."

Ten or twelve miles. That is how far away the town was that Ibrahim was pleading for — and, as his own plea will make plain, Lut (peace be upon him) was inside it.

## The pleading itself
