Ibn Kathir heads this passage **"The Dispute of Ibrahim over the People of Lut."** The ayah says he began to plead *with Us* — and Ibn Kathir supplies the sense in a parenthesis: *(Our messengers)*. The words were spoken to the angels standing in front of him; the appeal was to Allah.

What did the plea sound like? Ibn Kathir gives the account as **Saʿid bin Jubayr** narrated it concerning this verse. When Jibril and the angels with him came to Ibrahim, they said: *"Verily, we are going to destroy the people of this town"* (29:31).

> Ibrahim said to them, "Will you destroy a town that has three hundred believers in it?" They said, "No." He then said, "Will you destroy a town that has two hundred believers in it?" They said, "No." He said, "Will you destroy a town that has forty believers in it?" They said, "No." He then said, "Thirty?" They still replied, "No." This continued until he said, "Five?" They said, "No." Then he said, "What do you think if there is one Muslim man in the town, would you destroy it?" They said, "No."

Notice what he is arguing. He never asks that the crime be excused. Every single question is about the *innocent* — is there anyone in there worth sparing the place for? He works the number down from three hundred to one, and at each step the angels concede: no, such a town would not be destroyed. Having established that, he names the one he knows: *"But there is Lut in it."*

The reply is the hinge of the whole passage: *"We know better who is there. We will verily, save him and his family except his wife"* (29:32).

Ibn Kathir's closing line is worth sitting with: **"Therefore, Ibrahim remained silent and his soul was at rest."**

Read the sequence carefully, because the text puts the assurance first and the silence second. His whole plea had been built on the question of who was inside. He was answered by One who knows better than he does who is inside — and given a guarantee by name that Lut and his family would be saved. Then came the silence. And Ibn Kathir does not describe it as defeat: his soul was *at rest*.

*(A note on sourcing: this account comes from Saʿid bin Jubayr as quoted by Ibn Kathir. It is the report of an early authority, not a narration from the Prophet ﷺ.)*

## Ayah 75: three words for the kind of heart that does this

Right in the middle of the scene, Allah pauses to describe the man. The Arabic is three dense words — **ḥalīm, awwāh, munīb** — and our two sources render them slightly differently, which is itself instructive:

| Arabic | Translation before us | Ibn Kathir's rendering |
|---|---|---|
| ḥalīm | forbearing | forbearing |
| awwāh | tender-hearted | used to invoke Allah with humility |
| munīb | ever turning | repentant |

The first is agreed: **forbearing**. And forbearance is exactly what the scene shows — Ibrahim has just been told these people are finished, and he is still trying to slow the hand of punishment.

The second word is the hardest to carry into English, and the two renderings before us catch different sides of it: a **tenderness of heart**, and a **humility in calling upon Allah**. The third comes out as **ever turning** and as **repentant** — a man whose direction of travel is back toward Allah.

Ibn Kathir's own comment is plain and complete: *"This is a commendation for Ibrahim because of these beautiful characteristics."*

**Where this commendation sits is the point.** It comes *after* the pleading of ayah 74 and *before* the refusal of ayah 76. Allah praises him, in the middle, for a request that was not going to be granted. The plea was declined; the pleader was honoured. A prayer refused is not a prayer rejected — and mercy extended toward people who have earned none of it is here named as one of a prophet's beautiful characteristics.

## Ayah 76: "Plead no more"

*"O Abraham! Plead no more! Your Lord's decree has already come…"* Ibn Kathir renders the command as *"Forsake this"* — turn away from this line of argument.

His explanation of why: *"This means the decree was settled concerning them and the Word was already given that they should be destroyed. The evil torment was coming to them, that cannot be averted from wicked people."*

Two things are being said. First, **timing** — the matter had already passed out of the phase where intercession applies. Maʿārif states the angels' errand plainly: they were sent "to execute the punishment against these people." Second, **finality** — this torment, in the wording Ibn Kathir cites, "cannot be turned back."

And yet look at how the halt is delivered. He is called by name — *"O Ibrahim"* — and the decree is described to him as **your Lord's** command, *amru rabbika*. Even the sentence that closes the door addresses him as one belonging to his own Lord. It is a stop, not a scolding. And the man receiving it is the same man ayah 75 has just commended.

## Why the punishment was so severe

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the passage in its surah: Surah Hud "carries an account of different kinds of Divine punishments sent over past peoples because of their antagonism to prophets of the time," and these verses describe "the moral condition of the people of Sayyidna Lut and the severe punishment given to them."

On that moral condition Maʿārif is blunt. Beyond disbelief, these people were sunk in an evil "not found in the world before them, something even wild animals hate." That a man would pollute his honour and dignity with another man is "a curse the fallout from which is far more injurious than common fornication" — "therefore, the harsh punishment that descended on these people had never hit known practitioners of common acts of immodesty."

Maʿārif draws a principle out of this that reaches well beyond the episode: **"When He seizes a people in punishment, the punishment that He makes descend upon them is chosen to be congruous to their misdeed."** Even the form of the visit belonged to that fittingness — the angels, Maʿārif notes, "were sent in the form of handsome young men." The severity of ayah 76 is measured, not arbitrary.

## One more thing the angels' answer contains

Return to the guarantee that ended the dispute: *"We will verily, save him and his family **except his wife**."* Ibrahim had asked whether there were believers in the town; the angels answered with a knowledge finer than his — they knew precisely who was a believer and who merely lived in a believer's house.

Maʿārif names two exhibits in what it calls Allah's "open gallery of lessons full of the countless exhibits of His perfect power and eloquent wisdom." Ibrahim, Allah's friend, "come out as a prophet from the home of Azar, the idol-worshipper." And in the home of the honoured prophet Lut, a wife "who worked in league with disbelievers and opposed her prophet husband" — the one who, when the guests arrived, passed word about them to the depraved men of the town (Maʿārif, citing Qurtubi and Mazhari).

Nearness to a prophet saved no one. A household of disbelief doomed no one either.

## Living it

**Plead for people.** The ayah's own order is the lesson: the fear lifts, the good news lands, and the first use Ibrahim makes of that moment is to argue for a people the sources describe as sunk in disbelief and gross immodesty. When relief comes to you, that is the moment to intercede for someone else.

**Argue the way he argued.** He did not defend the sin; he searched for the innocent. That is a discipline worth copying whenever a whole community is being written off in one sentence.

**Then submit when the matter is Allah's.** There is a difference between the phase in which pleading is beautiful — ayah 75, where it is commended — and the phase in which the decree has gone forth — ayah 76. When Ibrahim was told that Allah knows better who is inside, he "remained silent and his soul was at rest." Not resignation. Rest.

**And take the three words of ayah 75 as a description to grow into:** forbearing; tender-hearted, calling on Allah with humility; and ever turning back to Him.

passages.title: Lot besieged by his own people
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Ayat 77–80 put us inside one night in the town of Lut (peace be upon him). Allah's angels arrive at his door in the form of human guests, the town comes running, and a prophet stands alone in the doorway — pleading, appealing to Allah, appealing to a host's honour — until he cries out that he has neither the strength nor the backing to hold them off.

What binds the four ayat is not just sequence but a tightening vice. Ayah 77 is dread before anything has happened. Ayah 78 is the assault, and Lut's desperate attempt to turn his people toward what is lawful. Ayah 79 is their flat, shameless refusal. Ayah 80 is a righteous man reaching the end of himself.

## The night these ayat belong to

Ibn Kathir sets the scene: these are the same angels who had just left Ibrahim, after informing him of their mission to destroy Lut's people — and they "set out to destroy Lut's people that very night." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the geography: Allah sent these angels, Jibra'il among them, first to Ibrahim in Palestine, and Lut's home lay some ten or twelve miles away.

So we, the readers, already know what Lut does not. The visitors at his door are not in danger. They *are* the punishment, walking.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a striking observation about the design behind the disguise: when Allah seizes a people in punishment, "the punishment that He makes descend upon them is chosen to be congruous to their misdeed" — and "on this occasion too, these angels of Allah were sent in the form of handsome young men." Ibn Kathir describes the same: they came "in the most handsome of forms… young men with handsome faces," and he calls this "a test from Allah that contained much wisdom and a firm evidence."

Qatadah reports a related instruction the angels were under: they "were ordered not to destroy them until their Prophet testified against them of this." The sentence was not to fall until the case had been proved on the ground, by the mouth of the prophet who lived among them.

## Ayah 77: a prophet with nowhere to turn

**سِيءَ بِهِمْ وَضَاقَ بِهِمْ ذَرْعًا** — Ibn Kathir renders the clause as a whole: "he was grieved on account of them and was concerned for them." Our translation gives it as "he was distressed." Two things are named together in that rendering — sorrow, and a weight of worry. Ibn Kathir expands it: "Their appearance saddened him (Lut) and he felt grief in his soul because of them."

Why? Ibn Kathir: "He was afraid that if he did not host them as his guests, someone else of his people would host them and harm them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up his position in four words — "He found himself in a fix" — and then sharpens it into a trap with no exit: "If he backed out from entertaining guests, it would be against his dignity as a prophet. If he took them in as his guests, then, he knew how evil and dirty his people were." The danger, it adds, was that his people "might storm his home and hurt the guests while he failed to defend them."

Then his own words: **هَٰذَا يَوْمٌ عَصِيبٌ** — "This is a distressful day." Ibn 'Abbas and others glossed this as "a severe test for him," because, as Ibn Kathir explains, "he knew that he would have to defend them and it would cause great problems for him."

**The walk home.** Qatadah preserves one of the most human details in the whole account. The angels came to Lut while he was on a piece of land that belonged to him, and asked to be hosted. He agreed — but he was shy before them, and walked in front of them on the way to his home. Trying to convince them to go away without withdrawing his hospitality outright, he said, "By Allah, I do not know any people on the face of the earth more wicked and disgusting than these people of this town." He walked on a little further and said it again. He kept doing this until he had repeated it four times.

Sit with that. A prophet cannot bring himself to say *don't come*, so he says *you don't know what you are walking into* — four times, hoping they will take the hint. And, as Qatadah notes, it was precisely this testimony of a prophet against his own people that had to be given before the destruction could fall.

**A house divided.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here on a wider lesson, saying that Allah has made this world "an open gallery of lessons" full of exhibits of His perfect power and wisdom. He brought Ibrahim, His friend, out as a prophet from the home of Azar the idol-worshipper — and in the home of the highly revered prophet Lut there was a wife "who worked in league with disbelievers and opposed her prophet husband." When the honoured guests arrived in the form of handsome young men, it was she who passed the information on to the corrupt men among his people (Qurtubi, Mazhari). Guidance is Allah's gift; it is not inherited, and it does not rub off from proximity.

## Ayah 78: the rush to the door

**وَجَاءَهُ قَوْمُهُ يُهْرَعُونَ إِلَيْهِ** — his people came *rushing* to him. Ibn Kathir explains the verb plainly: "they made haste and rushed due to their delight" at the new arrivals. This is not a mob stumbling out in confusion; it is eagerness.

Then the Qur'an slips in a whole history in one clause: **وَمِن قَبْلُ كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ السَّيِّئَاتِ** — "and since aforetime they used to commit crimes." Ibn Kathir: "this did not cease being their behavior until they were seized [by Allah's torment] and they were still in the same condition." The sin was not an incident. It was the settled shape of their lives, right up to the moment the punishment seized them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what that hardening cost them: "such was the curse of their evil deed that they had lost all sense of modesty and propriety, so much so that they did not hesitate to storm even the home of Sayyidna Lut for a purpose that sinister." Nothing was sacred to them any more — not a guest, not a prophet, not a home.

## "Here are my daughters, they are purer for you"

This is the hardest sentence in the passage, and the commentators read it in two ways.

**First reading — his own daughters, in marriage.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, holds that when Lut realised it was difficult to protect his guests, he tried to divert his people by telling them he would give his daughters in marriage to their chiefs if they would stop their evil-mongering. The marriage of a believing woman to a disbelieving man was permissible in that era; the practice continued into the early period of the Prophet ﷺ, who gave two of his daughters in marriage to 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab and Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi', though both of them were disbelievers. Verses came later prohibiting the marriage of Muslim women to disbelieving men as haram.

**Second reading — the women of the nation.** Mujahid said: "Actually, they were not his daughters, but they were from among his nation. Every Prophet is like a father to his nation." Ibn Kathir notes a similar statement reported from Qatadah and others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supports this reading with the ayah "The Prophet comes first with the believers against their own selves and his wives are (like) their mothers" (33:6), read together with the additional words in the rendition (qirāʾah, meaning a transmitted way of reciting) of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, "and he is [like] a father for them." On this reading Lut is saying: leave this evil habit, behave like gentlemen, marry girls from your own people and have them as your wives.

Both readings land in the same place, and Ibn Kathir names it: "This was his attempt to direct them to their women, for verily the Prophet is like a father for his nation. Therefore, he tries to guide them to that which is better for them in this life and the Hereafter." He points to the parallel wording elsewhere — "Go you in unto the males of the nation, and leave those whom Allah has created for you to be your wives" (26:165–166) — and to the town's own retort in another surah, "Did we not forbid you from entertaining any of the 'Ālamīn" (15:70), which Ibn Kathir explains as: didn't we forbid you from hosting male guests?

Notice the word **أَطْهَر**, "purer." Lut does not argue from custom or convenience. He puts the two paths side by side and pronounces a verdict on their moral quality.

Then three short movements, one after another:

- **فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ** — "So have Taqwa of Allah." *Taqwa* is the reverent awareness of Allah that holds a person back from what Allah has forbidden; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase simply "So, fear Allah," and reads it as a warning against divine punishment — which, unknown to them, had already arrived in his house in the form of his guests. Ibn Kathir's gloss is practical: "Accept what I command you by limiting the fulfillment of your desires to your women."
- **وَلَا تُخْزُونِ فِي ضَيْفِي** — "and disgrace me not with regard to my guests." Having appealed to Allah, he now appeals to their sense of a host's honour.
- **أَلَيْسَ مِنكُمْ رَجُلٌ رَّشِيدٌ** — "Is there not among you a single right-minded man?" Ibn Kathir: "Is there not a good man among you who will accept what I am enjoining upon you and abandon what I have forbidden for you?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: someone who would even *listen* to his plaint.

The question is left hanging. That silence is the verdict on the town.

## Ayah 79: an answer with no shame in it

**"Surely, you know that we have no need of your daughters, and indeed you know well what we want!"** Ibn Kathir unpacks both halves: "Verily, you know that we do not want our women, nor do we desire them," and then, "We only want males and you know that. So what need is there for you to continue speaking to us about this?"

What is chilling is what is missing. No denial. No embarrassment. No attempt to justify. They do not even bother to argue with a prophet — they tell him to stop wasting breath, because he already knows. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's judgement is blunt: "there was no trace of gentility or even humanness left in any of them."

## Ayah 80: "If only I had strength against you"

**لَوْ أَنَّ لِي بِكُمْ قُوَّةً أَوْ آوِي إِلَىٰ رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ** — "Would that I had strength to overpower you, or that I could betake myself to some powerful support."

Ibn Kathir reads it as a threat wrung out of a man with nothing to threaten with: "I would surely have made an example of you and done [harm] to you from myself and my family." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: only if I had enough strength in me to stand against this onslaught, "or that I had the backing of some strong group who would have helped me get rid of these oppressors."

'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas fills in the physical scene: when the people mobbed his home, Lut had closed the entrance door, and the whole conversation was going on from behind it. The angels were inside. The mob was threatening to jump the walls, barge in and break the door down. It was at that exact moment that these words came to his lips.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir reports from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah's mercy be upon Lut, for verily, he betook himself to a powerful support — [meaning Allah, the Mighty and Sublime] — Allah did not send any Prophet after him, except amidst [an influential family] among his people." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that a hadith on this appears in the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, with the wording that Lut "was compelled to seek the protection of some strong group," and that the report in *Tirmidhi* carries the additional sentence that after Lut, Allah sent no prophet whose clan or tribe was not his supporter.

There is enormous tenderness in that "May Allah's mercy be upon Lut." The Prophet ﷺ does not scold him for the cry; he honours the pain of it. And the hadith names what Lut, from behind his own door, could not see: the "powerful support" he was reaching for was Allah, the Mighty and Sublime — not a clan, not a fighting force, but his Lord, on whom he was already relying. Nor was Allah's help far away: the very guests he was straining to protect were messengers Allah had already sent, and Lut simply did not yet know it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws the line forward: this is exactly why the Prophet ﷺ, though the disbelieving Quraysh did everything they could against him, always had his own clan behind him — Banu Hashim as a whole sided with him in the boycott the Quraysh imposed, cutting off essential supplies, even though they did not agree with him in religion.

And there the passage leaves us: a prophet at a barred door, out of strength, calling for a support he cannot see.

## What this passage asks of us

**Guard the guest.** Lut's entire crisis is that he would not hand over a guest. He would face a town alone rather than let someone under his roof be harmed. That is the standard of hospitality this passage quietly sets.

**Be the one right-minded man.** "Is there not among you a single right-minded man?" — the question that got no answer. Ibn Kathir's gloss makes it practical: a man who accepts what is enjoined and abandons what is forbidden. In a crowd that has stopped feeling shame, being that single person is itself the whole test.

**Sin becomes a condition.** Ibn Kathir's remark on ayah 78 — that this never ceased to be their behaviour until the punishment seized them — is a warning about repeated sin. What begins as an act ends as an identity, and by then a prophet at the door cannot reach you.

**Lean on the strong pillar.** Lut wished for a *rukn shadīd*, a powerful support, in the moment his own strength ran out. The hadith names what that support truly was: Allah. When a believer's own resources are exhausted and no one is standing with him, the support he is reaching for is not absent — and Allah's help may already be at work in ways he cannot yet see.

passages.title: The angels reveal themselves; the cities overturned
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the turning point of the story of Lūṭ (peace be upon him): the visitors at his door stop being helpless guests and reveal themselves as angels of Allah, his household is led out of the city under cover of night, and at sunrise the towns are lifted up and turned over. What holds the passage together is a single truth told in three movements — rescue and ruin arrive by one and the same command. Ayah 81 is the rescue, ayah 82 is the ruin, and the close of ayah 83 turns the whole scene outward to face anyone who does what those people did.

## The night the door held

To feel ayah 81, you have to hear ayah 80 still ringing. Lūṭ, alone at his door with a mob outside, had just said: **"Would that I had strength to overpower you, or that I could betake myself to some powerful support."** Ibn Kathir explains the sense: *I would surely have made an example of you and done harm to you from myself and my family.* It is the cry of a man with no clan behind him to defend his honour, nothing but his own two hands.

Ibn Kathir mentions here a hadith reported from Abu Hurayrah — he does not name the collection it comes from — in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that may Allah's mercy be upon Lūṭ, for he was already betaking himself to a powerful support, meaning Allah the Mighty and Sublime; and that Allah sent no prophet after him except amidst an influential family among his people. Two things are packed into that. First, the support Lūṭ was wishing for was one he already had: he was leaning on Allah, the strongest support in existence. Second, his loneliness was so severe that Allah did not repeat it — every prophet sent after him was given the shelter of standing kin.

So ayah 81 opens exactly at the point where a human being runs out.

**قَالُوا يَا لُوطُ إِنَّا رُسُلُ رَبِّكَ** — *"They said: O Lūṭ! Verily we are the messengers from your Lord."* Notice the wording: not "messengers" in the abstract, but **messengers of *your* Lord**. The reassurance is personal before it is cosmic. Ibn Kathir notes that with these words the angels informed him that they were the messengers of Allah sent to those people, and that his people would not be able to reach him with any harm — **لَن يَصِلُوا إِلَيْكَ**, *"They shall not reach you."* The threat that had felt total a moment earlier was never even a possibility.

And it was answered in front of him. Ibn Kathir sets the scene: all of this was being said while Lūṭ's people stood at his door, trying to rush it from every side, with Lūṭ at the door repelling them, deterring them, trying to hold them back from what they intended — and they would not listen; instead they threatened him and sought to intimidate him. At that point Jibrīl came out to them and struck them in their faces with his wing. The blow blinded their eyes and they fell back, unable to see their way. Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: **"And they indeed sought to shame his guest. So We blinded their eyes: Then taste you My torment and My warnings"** (54:37).

The man who wished for strength was, at that instant, the most heavily defended man on earth.

## Walk out in the dark — and do not turn around

The rescue comes as a set of instructions, and each one carries weight.

**فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ اللَّيْلِ** — *"So travel with your family in a part of the night."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "move with your family in a part of night"; Ibn Kathir specifies that they were commanded to travel during the last part of the night. The departure is quiet, in darkness, before the deadline.

Lūṭ was to walk at the back. Ibn Kathir notes that he was told to follow his family from behind — in this way it would be as though he were driving them along, the way a cattle herder drives his herd. A herder walks behind so that nobody straggles and nobody is lost. Even in flight, the prophet's posture is one of care for those in his charge.

**وَلَا يَلْتَفِتْ مِنكُمْ أَحَدٌ** — *"and let not any of you look back."* This is not a superstition about glances. Ibn Kathir gives the practical meaning: *if you hear the sound of what befalls them, do not rush toward that disturbing noise; rather, continue leaving.* The instinct being forbidden is a deeply human one — the pull to turn back toward a catastrophe, to look at it, to grieve over it, to move toward the crash. Once Allah's command has fallen on a people, the believer's job is to keep walking.

Then the exception: **إِلَّا امْرَأَتَكَ** — *"but your wife."* The Arabic is compressed, and the commentators divide over what exactly is being excepted.

- **Most of the scholars**, Ibn Kathir reports, said this means she would not travel by night at all — she did not go out with Lūṭ, but stayed in her house and was destroyed.
- **Others** said the exception attaches to the looking back: she left with them, and when she heard the inevitable destruction she turned and looked, and said, "O my people!" — and a stone came down from the sky and killed her.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents both readings side by side in the same way: the phrase could mean that he was not to take his wife along at all, or that she was to go along as part of his family but would not obey the instruction not to look back. Citing Qurtubi and Mazhari, it notes that according to some reports this second possibility is what happened: she started off with the others, but when she heard the big bang of the punishment given to her people she looked back and felt sorry at their destruction — and at that moment there came a splintered rock and finished her off like the others.

Either way the lesson is the same and sobering: sharing a prophet's house and his name saved nobody. And on the second reading, it was precisely her turning back toward the people she was being taken away from that undid her.

## The appointment, named and kept

Lūṭ, after a night like that, wanted it over. Ibn Kathir says that the angels brought the destruction of his people close to him as *good news*, because he had said to them: "Destroy them in this very hour." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same — he wished the punishment would come sooner.

Their answer is **إِنَّ مَوْعِدَهُمُ الصُّبْحُ ۚ أَلَيْسَ الصُّبْحُ بِقَرِيبٍ** — *"Indeed, morning is their appointed time. Is not the morning near?"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the first half as *the deadline of the punishment is the morning*. Two things are said gently at once: the punishment has a fixed appointment, and the wait is short. It is the tone of someone telling a person in pain that the hour has already been set and is almost here.

And when ayah 82 opens — **فَلَمَّا جَاءَ أَمْرُنَا**, *"So when Our commandment came"* — Ibn Kathir states plainly that this happened at sunrise. The appointment named in ayah 81 is the appointment kept in ayah 82, to the hour.

## The towns turned over

**جَعَلْنَا عَالِيَهَا سَافِلَهَا** — *"We turned it upside down."* Ibn Kathir identifies the place as the city of Sadūm (Sodom), and compares the moment to Allah's words **"So there covered them that which did cover"** (53:54).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture from the reports: these habitations were composed of four major towns, and elsewhere in the Qur'an they are named **al-muʾtafikāt**, "the towns overturned" (9:70, 69:9). When the divine command came, the archangel Jibrāʼīl al-Amīn dissected with his wing the base of the land mass holding all those towns, and raised the whole of it upwards in such a way that everything stayed exactly where it was — even water in a water vessel. It was against a backdrop of human, animal and canine voices coming from the sky that he heaved these habitations straight up towards the sky, and then threw the whole thing back down upside down. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the point that makes this more than spectacle: it was done *as appropriate to and as called for by the evil they indulged in*. The shape of the ruin answered the shape of the sin.

## Three words for the stones

Ayah 82 continues: *"and rained on them stones of clay, in an array"*; ayah 83 opens **مُّسَوَّمَةً عِندَ رَبِّكَ**, *"marked from your Lord."* Three terms carry the whole image.

**سِجِّيل (sijjīl).** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and others that *sijjīl* is a Persian word meaning stones made of clay. Some scholars said it derives from *sang*, meaning a stone; others said it means *wakīl*, which is clay. Ibn Kathir cross-references **"the stones of clay"** (51:33), explaining that this means clay made into strong, hard stone — some said baked clay. He also quotes al-Bukhari: *"Sijjīl means that which is big and strong."* Clay is the humblest, softest material there is; at Allah's command it becomes the instrument that ends a civilisation.

**مَّنضُود (manḍūd), "in an array."** Ibn Kathir gives two explanations from the scholars. Some said it means the stones were arranged in the heavens and prepared for that destruction — stockpiled and ready, waiting on a decision already taken. Others said the word means that some of the stones followed others in their descent upon the people of Lūṭ.

**مُّسَوَّمَة (musawwamah), "marked."** Ibn Kathir explains that the stones were marked and sealed, all of them having the names of their victims written on them. Qatādah and ʿIkrimah both said that *musawwamah* means each stone was encompassed by a sprinkling of red colouring.

Ibn Kathir then reports what the commentators said about how it fell: the shower descended upon the people of the town and upon the various villages around it. One of them would be speaking with some people when a stone struck him from the sky and killed him while he stood among them. The stones followed them, striking people in the entire land until they were all destroyed — not a single one of them remained.

Put the three words together and the theology is unmistakable. This was not a natural disaster that happened to hit a wicked town. The material was prepared in advance, the descent was ordered, and every stone carried the name of the one it was for. Nothing about it was blind.

## "And they are not ever far from the wrongdoers"

**وَمَا هِيَ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ بِبَعِيدٍ.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line, and it changes the passage from history into address: *this vengeance of Allah is not far from similar wrongdoers.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the clause the same way, and is specific about its purpose: coming at the end of ayah 83, after the actual punishment that struck the people of Lūṭ has been described, it was said in order to warn the contemporary peoples of the world. Its meaning is that people who insist upon indulging in this shameful act should not consider themselves very far from this punishment — it can come even today. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the Prophet ﷺ said that even in his Ummah some people would do what the people of Lūṭ used to do, and that when this starts happening, then wait, for they too would be subjected to the same punishment that was inflicted on the people of Lūṭ. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes this without naming the collection it comes from.)

Ibn Kathir, under this same phrase, mentions a hadith **of the Sunan collections**, from Ibn ʿAbbās, which he attributed to the Prophet ﷺ: *"Whoever you find doing the deed of Lūṭ's people, then kill the doer and the one who allows it to be done to him."*

## Living it

The passage is not only a warning; it is also a description of how Allah treats those He is rescuing, and there is a great deal in it to hold onto.

**Help can be closer than it looks.** Lūṭ wished aloud for a powerful support — and the hadith Ibn Kathir reports says he was already resorting to the strongest support there is, Allah Himself. The messengers of his Lord were in his house at that very moment, before they had told him who they were.

**"They shall not reach you" is a real sentence.** What Allah has not permitted to reach you will not reach you, however loud it is at the door.

**Do not turn back toward the wreckage.** The command in ayah 81 — keep walking, do not rush toward the noise — is practical guidance about leaving behind what Allah has told you to leave. On the reading in which Lūṭ's wife set out and then turned, half-leaving is exactly what undid her.

**Nearness to righteous people is not itself salvation.** She was the wife of a prophet, and she was not spared.

**The appointment is fixed, and it is near.** "Is not the morning near?" was spoken to a man begging for the wait to end — and morning came exactly as promised, at sunrise. Allah's timing is neither late nor arbitrary, and impatience does not move it.

**And the last clause is turned outward.** Ibn Kathir reads it as saying that this vengeance is not far from wrongdoers like them; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as a warning that those who persist in this act should not think themselves far from that punishment — it can come even today. The stones that fell on Sadūm carried names. The ayah ends by telling the reader not to assume his own is not among them.

passages.title: Shu'aib on honest measure and lawful gain
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat carry the opening of Shu'aib's call to the people of Madyan — peace be upon him — and they hold together as one continuous speech. He begins where every prophet begins, with the worship of Allah alone (ayah 84); he moves straight from there to the scales in the marketplace (ayah 85); and he closes by telling them where real profit actually lies and reminding them that he is not the one watching them (ayah 86). Faith, honest trade, and sincerity: in this passage they are not three subjects but one.

## Who were Madyan, and why "their brother"?

Ibn Kathir describes the people of Madyan as a tribe of Arabs who lived between the land of al-Hijaz and ash-Sham, close to the land of Ma'an; their land took the name of their tribe, and so was called Madyan. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a complementary account: Madyan was the name of a town settled by Madyan ibn Ibrahim, and its location has been identified with Ma'an in present-day Jordan, the townspeople themselves coming to be called Madyan.

Ayah 84 does not say "and to Madyan We sent Shu'aib" but **"their brother Shu'aib."** Both commentaries pause on that word. Ibn Kathir notes that Shu'aib was of the noblest of them in lineage, and that it is for this reason Allah says "their brother." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the mercy in it: by calling him the brother of Madyan, the Qur'an hints that Allah Ta'ala sent His messenger to those people *from among them*, so that they would feel familiar with him and find it easier to accept his teaching. The warner was not a stranger dropped among them. He was one of their own, and of the noblest lineage among them — which is precisely what makes his rejection later so damning.

What did they worship? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that they were mushriks — those who associate partners in the divinity of Allah — and that they worshipped trees. This is pointed to by the word *al-'aikah* (trees) in the Qur'an, which is why the people of Madyan also carry the title *aṣḥāb al-'aikah*, "the people of the aikah — the trees" (see 15:78, 26:176, 38:13, 50:14).

## Why the worship of Allah alone comes first — and why the scales come immediately second

In ayah 84 Shu'aib says: *"O my people, worship Allah. You have no god other than Him. And do not lessen the measure and the weight."* Ibn Kathir summarises the two halves exactly: he commanded them to worship Allah alone without associating any partners with Him, and he prohibited them from cheating in their weights and measures in business. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in the first half he was inviting them to belief in the Oneness of Allah — *tawḥīd*, the Arabic term for holding Allah to be One, alone deserving of worship — precisely because they were mushriks who worshipped trees.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws an important principle out of this ordering, under a "Special Note." *Kufr* — disbelief, the rejection of faith — and *shirk* — assigning partners to Allah — are the roots of all sins. People soaked in them are usually the first to be invited to believe; faith comes before consideration can be given to social transactions and individual deeds, because whether a people are delivered in this world or deserve punishment is itself decided on the basis of faith or denial. That is the pattern across all the prophetic accounts in the Qur'an — with, Maʿārif notes, two exceptions. The people of Lut and the people of Shu'aib were punished for their disbelief *and* for a specific evil practice: for the people of Lut, the practice mentioned as the reason their habitation was overturned; for the people of Shu'aib, their habit of weighing less and measuring short.

Sit with that. Of all the sins a nation can commit, cheating at the scales is placed alongside the sin of Lut's people as a cause of destruction in its own right. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says these two are the most hated and grave of sins, and explains why: obviously, the reason is that they bring serious loss upon the entire human race, leaving the world populated by it in a disorder of ominous proportions. That is the measure of it — not a small dishonesty between two people at a stall, but an injury reaching the whole of humanity.

## "I see you in prosperity" — the argument from blessing

The second half of ayah 84 is the emotional heart of Shu'aib's appeal: *"I see you in prosperity, and verily I fear for you the torment of an encompassing Day."*

Ibn Kathir explains "in prosperity" as meaning *in your livelihood and your provisions* — and reads the warning as: I fear that you will be deprived of this bounty you are enjoying, by violating Allah's prohibitions.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls these words eloquent, and unfolds the logic inside them. Shu'aib found his people living comfortably. They were not poor, not hungry, not financially straitened — which could otherwise have been offered as some reason for taking recourse to such a cursed practice. They had no excuse of need. And since they were *already* blessed by Allah Ta'ala, that very blessing required of them that they not subject His creation to injustice. This is prophetic compassion working as argument: *look at what He has already given you; now look at what you are doing to His servants for a few grains more.*

Then the warning: *"the torment of a Day encompassing."* Here the two commentaries read differently, and it is worth keeping both rather than flattening them into one. Ibn Kathir takes the phrase to mean the abode of the Hereafter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that it may mean the punishment of the Hereafter *and* the punishment of this present world too, and that worldly punishments may come in different kinds. The lowest of them, it says, would be that they simply lose the prosperity they have, or fall victim to famines and price rises. Maʿārif cites the teaching of the Holy Prophet ﷺ that when a people start lessening weights and measures, Allah Ta'ala makes them suffer the punishment of famine and price hikes. (The commentary quotes this without naming a collection, so it is passed on here only as the commentary gives it.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells us the end of the story in advance: they persisted in their denial and obstinacy, and as a consequence all those people were destroyed through a severe punishment.

## Ayah 85: from "do not take away" to "give in full"

Ayah 84 said *do not lessen* the measure and the weight. Ayah 85 says *"O my people, perfect the measure and the balance with justice, and do not make the people short of their things, and do not go about the earth spreading disorder."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices what looks at first like repetition and shows it is not: obviously, the very prohibition of weighing and measuring short already makes weighing and measuring in full necessary — but to emphasise it further, Shu'aib states it as a positive command. This is worth pausing on. A prohibition can be satisfied by doing nothing; a command must be actively fulfilled. "Do not cheat" leaves a person passive and technically clean. "Give it full, with justice" makes honesty a duty you perform, not merely a crime you avoid. The two words *al-mikyāl* and *al-mīzān* name the two instruments of trade that the commentaries keep pairing — what is measured out, and what is weighed on a balance — and *bil-qisṭ*, "with justice," is the standard by which both are to be handled.

Ibn Kathir adds a detail that closes the last loophole. Shu'aib first prohibited them from cheating in business by decreasing the weights whenever they *gave* products to people; then he commanded them to give just measure and weight **whether they were giving or receiving** in transactions. The dishonest merchant has two scales, or one scale used two ways: generous when he takes in, stingy when he hands out. The command covers both directions of every transaction.

Then the phrase widens: *do not make the people short of their things.* Not "short of their grain" — short of *their things*, whatever is theirs. The same clause is rendered, in the translation of the ayah quoted at the head of Ibn Kathir's commentary, as *reduce not the things that are due to the people.* If that is the principle — not a rule about grain but a rule about what is owed — it is hard to confine it to the marketplace; it would reach any arrangement in which someone is owed something.

And the last clause of ayah 85 — *do not go about the earth spreading disorder* — has a concrete referent in Ibn Kathir's reading. He states that Shu'aib forbade them from causing mischief and corruption in the land, and that this was due to their practice of highway robbery along the roads. So the picture of this people fills in: shirk in their worship, fraud in their shops, and banditry on their roads. A society dishonest at the scale was also a society unsafe on the highway.

## Ayah 86: "What Allah leaves is better for you"

*"What is left by Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a guardian over you."*

The phrase is *baqiyyat Allah* — "what Allah leaves." Ibn Kathir reports the explanation of Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir, who glosses it as what is left by Allah *after giving the rights of the people*: what you gain from your successful business dealings in which you have given just measure is better for you than wrongfully taking the wealth of the people. Ibn Jarir states that this understanding has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase in the same direction: whatever is left with you by Allah is better for you, if you are believers.

This is the answer to the objection every cheat has ready: *but I will earn less.* The ayah does not deny the arithmetic; it denies the accounting. The smaller pile that Allah leaves in your hand after everyone's right has been paid out of it is the better pile. Ibn Kathir reinforces this by pointing to a parallel verse: *"Say: Not equal are the evil and the good, even though the abundance of the evil may please you"* (5:100). The Qur'an concedes the very thing the cheat is relying on — the impure heap really can be bigger, and it really can be impressive — and then says the categories are not comparable, so the size was never the question.

**"If you are believers."** The condition is placed exactly where it bites. This argument only lands on someone who accepts that Allah's account is the real one. To a person who believes only in the till at the end of the day, "less is better" is nonsense. To a believer it is simple sense.

**"And I am not a guardian over you."** Ibn Kathir explains this as: a watcher over you people — in other words, *do this for Allah, and not to be seen by the people.* This is the quiet climax of the whole passage. Shu'aib deliberately steps out of the role of enforcement. He is not the inspector, not the trading-standards officer, not the reason to behave. If honesty at the scale depends on a man watching, it will last exactly as long as he is looking. The only measure that stays true in an empty shop is the one held by someone who knows Allah sees.

## Living it

The passage asks for four things, and each of them is stated in it:

- **Get the foundation right first.** Ayah 84 puts *worship Allah alone* before *do not lessen the measure*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's "Special Note" is explicit that faith precedes the reform of transactions and deeds.
- **Be exact in both directions.** Ibn Kathir: just measure and weight whether giving or receiving. Not merely *don't defraud* — actively *give it full, with justice* (ayah 85).
- **Do not shave people's rights anywhere.** *Do not make the people short of their things* is broader than grain and gold — the ayah is also rendered *reduce not the things that are due to the people.*
- **Take the smaller, cleaner gain and be content.** *Baqiyyat Allah khayrun lakum* (ayah 86), on the understanding of Ibn 'Abbas as transmitted by Ibn Jarir: the honest earning is better than what is seized from people's wealth — and do it for Allah, not for the eye of any watcher.

The passage also carries a warning worth hearing in a prosperous age. In Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading of ayah 84, Shu'aib's people were not poor, hungry, or financially straitened — they had no excuse of need — and were still taking from others. Blessing does not excuse injustice; being already blessed by Allah Ta'ala was precisely what required them not to subject His creation to injustice. And on that same reading, the lowest of the worldly punishments for it may simply be that they lose the prosperity they had.

passages.title: Midian mocks his prayer; Shu'aib's reasoned reply
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Ayat 87–90 record an exchange between Shu'aib عليه السلام and his people at Madyan. Their reply in ayah 87 tells us what he had been asking of them: that they leave what their fathers used to worship — Ibn Kathir glosses this as the idols and statues — and that they stop doing as they pleased with their wealth, which Ibn Kathir explains as their practice of lightening the scales. They answer him with a sneer (87); he answers the sneer with reasoning, self-examination, a warning, and finally an open door (88–90). What binds the four ayat together is that contrast: mockery met by counsel. Not one word of his reply is retaliation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that the Prophet ﷺ said of Shu'aib that he was an orator among prophets — his eloquence was exceptional, and he went to its farthest limits in order to make his people understand his message and take to the right path. And even after having listened to him, they threw taunts at him and made fun of him.

## The taunt (ayah 87)

"O Shu'aib! Does your **salah** command you that we give up what our fathers used to worship, or that we give up doing what we like with our property?"

Notice what they aim at. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Shu'aib's salah was well known among his people because he was constantly devoted to it — so they referred to it tauntingly, in the sense that — Allah forbid — his salah was what taught him to say all those "wild" things. Al-A'mash said that "your salah" here means *your reading* — his recitation, the sound of his devotions.

Their objection comes in two halves, and the pairing is the whole point:

1. **"…that we give up what our fathers used to worship"** — Ibn Kathir: meaning the idols and statues. This is the religious half, and the reason they give for holding to it is inheritance: not that the idols are true, only that the fathers held them.

2. **"…or that we do with our property what we like"** — Ibn Kathir renders their meaning bluntly: *"Should we abandon our practice of lightening the scales because of your statement? This is our wealth and we will do with it as we please."* Ath-Thawri said that in this half "they were speaking in reference to the paying of Zakah (charity)."

Then the sting in the tail: **"Verily, you are the forbearer, right-minded!"** — *al-ḥalīm ar-rashīd*. The words themselves are praise: forbearance, and sound right-mindedness. But Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Maymun bin Mihran, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Aslam and Ibn Jarir: "These enemies of Allah were only saying this in mockery. May Allah disfigure them and curse them from ever receiving His mercy. And verily, He did so." Words of honour, used as a jab.

**The taunt that was accidentally correct.** Al-Hasan heard their line "Does your salah command you that we give up what our fathers used to worship" and said: "By Allah, this means that his prayer commanded them to abandon what their fathers used to worship." They put it as an absurdity. Al-Hasan read it as a plain statement of fact — that this is exactly what such a prayer does.

## The wall they built between religion and money

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the assumption buried in their question, and it is the most contemporary thing in the passage. From what they said, we learn that **they too thought that religion is restricted to acts of worship, and that it had nothing to do with material dealings.** Let everyone earn and spend one's wealth at will; placing any restriction on that is no job of religion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then observes that many people, even in this time of ours, generally believe exactly this, in total ignorance of the real fact.

So the quarrel at Madyan was not really about whether Shu'aib prayed. They were content to let him keep his salah; what they would not accept was that religion had any say over their scales.

## Shu'aib's reply (ayah 88)

He had just been mocked. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that his counsel had been good counsel based on earnest fellow feeling, and that their sarcasm was biting — yet he heard their caustic comments and still turned to them with the same empathy, trying once more to make them see the truth. The reply moves in five short steps.

**1. "Consider if I stand on a clear proof (bayyinah) from my Lord."** Ibn Kathir: meaning, upon clear guidance in that which I am calling to. He does not begin by attacking their idols; he begins by asking them to weigh the possibility that he is right. The verb the ayah uses, *ara'aytum*, is rendered "consider" and, in Ibn Kathir's phrasing, "do you see, O my people" — an invitation to look at the claim with him.

**2. "…and He has provided me from Himself a good provision."** Two explanations are reported, and Ibn Kathir accepts both: it has been said that he meant **prophethood**, and it has been said that he meant **lawful provisions** — "it seems that the verse carries both meanings." Ibn Kathir's own rendering of the ayah supplies the conclusion the sentence is driving at: *shall I corrupt it by mixing it with the unlawfully earned money?* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same point positively — Shu'aib had been given good provision for his material life *and* the light of revelation and spiritual insight; with these wonderful assets in his hands, how could he ever think of becoming like them, willingly embracing error and injustice, and thus failing to bring the truth home to them?

**3. "I do not wish to go behind your backs and do the very thing I forbid you."** Ath-Thawri explains it as: I do not forbid you from something and at the same time contradict my own prohibitions in secret behind your backs, doing what I have forbidden. Qatadah says the same: "I do not forbid you all from something while I do it myself." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson for anyone who calls to Allah — the way a preacher of religion conducts his life has a major role in what he preaches, and what a preacher does not himself practise produces no effect on others.

**4. "I only desire reform (iṣlāḥ), as much as I am able."** Ibn Kathir: "In that which I command and forbid you, I only want to correct your affair as much as I am able." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "I want to do nothing but to set things right as far as I can." Two things are worth pausing on. First, what he names as his aim is *iṣlāḥ* — reform, setting right. Second, the qualifier *mā istaṭa't*, "as far as I can": the limit he places is on his own capacity, not on their response.

**5. "And my tawfīq is only from Allah; in Him I trust, and to Him I turn."** On *tawfīqī*, Ibn Kathir explains: "in whatever I intend that agrees with the truth"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "my ability to do things comes from none but Allah." Between the two glosses: that his intention should land on what is actually true, and that he should be able to act on it at all, comes from Allah alone. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this is why the sentence is here — even the reforming effort of step 4 was not by his personal choice and volition. "In Him I put my trust" — Ibn Kathir: this means in all of my affairs. And *wa ilayhi unīb*, "and unto Him I repent" — meaning "I return," as said by Mujahid and others.

Hold the two speeches side by side. They said: **we do with our wealth whatever we wish.** He said: **my ability to do things comes from none but Allah.** One sentence claims volition; the other hands it back.

## The warning (ayah 89)

"O my people, do not let my **shiqāq** bring upon you the like of what struck the people of Nuh, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih — and the people of Lut are not far from you."

The word *shiqāqī* is kept in Arabic here because the commentators explain it by its force in this context rather than by a single English equivalent. Ibn Kathir reads the ayah: "Do not let your hatred and enmity of me cause you to persist in your corruption and disbelief. If you continue this way, you will suffer the same vengeance and torment that overcame Nuh's people, Hud's people, Salih's people and Lut's people." Qatadah puts it in one line: "Do not be influenced by your differing with me." As-Suddi: "your enmity of me should not lead you to continue in misguidance and disbelief, or else you will be afflicted by what afflicted them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "let not your hostility towards me cause you to suffer…"

All three glosses turn on the same hinge, and it is worth sitting with. The warning is not simply *do not oppose me*. It is: do not let what you feel about me carry you on into persisting in the thing that will destroy you.

**The roll-call, and why Lut is placed last.** Three destroyed nations are named in a row, then the people of Lut are set apart with a separate clause: *"and the people of Lut are not far off from you."* On this last phrase Ibn Kathir reports two views — that it refers to the period of **time**, and that it refers to **place** — and concludes: "Actually, the verse carries both meanings." Qatadah took the time-sense: "This means that they were only destroyed before you yesterday." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes both: the overturned habitations of the people of Lut عليه السلام were close to Madyan where they were, and in terms of time the punishment that came upon them was very close — near enough that from this they could learn their lesson and leave their obstinacy.

## The door left open (ayah 90)

"And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Truly my Lord is Most Merciful, Most Loving."

Ibn Kathir reads the two commands as covering two different stretches of time: **ask forgiveness of your Lord** from the previous sins, and **turn unto Him in repentance** in whatever evil actions you may encounter in the future. Repentance here is not only the settling of a past account; it is turned forward as well.

And the passage that began with a sneer ends on two of Allah's names. *Raḥīm* — Most Merciful. *Wadūd* — Most Loving. Ibn Kathir specifies: to those who repent. We affirm these names as they came, without likening Allah's mercy or love to anything in creation and without emptying the words of their meaning. The ayah's own wording also moves from "your Lord" in the command to "**my** Lord" in the statement about mercy.

For a people who had just mocked him to his face, that ending is remarkable. Warning and invitation in the same breath, and the invitation gets the last word.

## What happened afterwards

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān continues the story past this passage. Hearing this, his people were enraged, and said that had it not been for the support he had from his clan, they would have stoned him to death. Despite the threat, Shu'aib عليه السلام, true to his mettle as a prophet, did not hesitate to tell them that they feared his clan all right, but had no fear of Allah, who holds everything in His power. Finally, when his people would not listen to anything said to them, he told them that they could now wait for the punishment. After that, Allah Taʿālā took Shu'aib عليه السلام and those who had believed in him out of that habitation, as is the Divine practice, and the rest of them were destroyed instantly at the harsh Cry of Jibra'il عليه السلام.

## Living it

**Short measure is bigger than short measure.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that one of the reasons punishment fell on Shu'aib's people was their practice of weighing and measuring less than due — *taṭfīf*. The Qur'an describes the severe punishment for this in the surah that opens: *"Woe to those who give less"* (83:1), and there is a consensus of the entire Muslim Ummah that doing so is strictly ḥarām. Quoting a saying of Sayyidna 'Umar رضي الله عنه, Imam Malik has said in the Muwaṭṭaʼ that weighing and measuring less essentially means **that someone does not fulfil the right of another person due on him, fully and duly** — in fact, makes it less, whether it happens to be something given by weight, or by measure, or something of another kind. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies this without softening it: if an employee falls short in performing an assigned duty, or an office worker or labourer cuts his working hours short or fails to fulfil his job assignment as due, they are all counted in this category. And it turns the blade inward: anyone who does not perform his salah with due consideration of everything obligatory in it has also committed the crime of this taṭfīf. May Allah keep all of us protected from it.

**Shaving value off what circulates.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Tafsir al-Qurtubi that Shu'aib's people would save gold and silver by trimming the edges of the gold and silver coins — dinar and dirham — circulating in the country as official currency, and would then channel those coins back into circulation at par value; Shu'aib عليه السلام prohibited them from doing so. It is also reported in Hadith that the Prophet ﷺ declared the chipping of the coins of an Islamic state to be ḥarām. The tafsir authority Zayd ibn Aslam said exactly this when explaining the verse about the "nine family heads spreading corruption in the land and not correcting their ways" (27:48): these people of the city used to chip off gold and silver from dinar and dirham coins and ran a profitable business of their own through this source — something the Qur'an calls a great corruption. Qurtubi also records that during the Khilafah of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz رحمه الله someone was arrested while cutting a dirham coin; he was awarded a punishment of lashes and paraded around with his head shaved.

Running through all of it is the "real fact" Madyan could not accept: religion is not restricted to acts of worship, and it does not leave material dealings alone.

**For anyone who calls others to good,** ayah 88 is a working manual. Do not forbid in public what you allow yourself in private. Aim at setting things right. Do what you can, and let "as much as I am able" be the honest measure of the duty. Ask Allah for *tawfīq* rather than banking on your own eloquence — Shu'aib was an orator among prophets and still said that his ability to do things comes from none but Allah. And when you are mocked, answer as he did: with reasons, with a warning given out of fellow feeling, and with the door to forgiveness held open.

passages.title: Threats, defiance, and the end of Midian
passages.tafsir:
This is the final exchange between Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) and the people of Madyan (Midian). In ayah 91 they answer his long appeal with contempt and a threat; in ayah 92 he answers them without flinching; in ayah 93 he tells them to carry on as they are and to wait; and in ayat 94–95 the waiting ends.

## The setting: a warning they had just heard

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out what came immediately before. After giving them his good counsel, Shuʿayb warned them of the punishment of Allah: "And O my people, let not your hostility towards me cause you to suffer what was suffered by the people of Nūḥ, or the people of Hūd, or the people of Ṣāliḥ. And the people of Lūṭ are not far from you."

That last phrase, Maʿārif explains, is pointed in two ways. The overturned settlements of the people of Lūṭ (peace be upon him) were close to Madyan, where these people lived; and in terms of time, the punishment that had come upon them was very recent. From this, Maʿārif notes, they could have taken their lesson and left their obstinacy.

Hearing this, Maʿārif says, his people were enraged. Ayah 91 is what the rage said.

## Ayah 91: three things said in one breath

**"We do not comprehend much of what you say."** Ibn Kathīr glosses it plainly: *this means that we do not comprehend*, and takes *kathīran*, "much," to mean "most of what you say."

Set beside that the remark Ibn Kathīr records from ath-Thawrī at exactly this point: Shuʿayb "was called the orator of the Prophets." The prophet remembered for his speech is the one his townsmen say they cannot follow.

**"And we see you weak among us."** Ibn Kathīr gives two early readings. As-Suddī said they meant, "You are only one person." Abū Rawq said they meant, "You are despised, because your tribe is not upon your religion." Either way, they are measuring him by numbers and by backing.

**"Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you."** *Rahṭ*, says Ibn Kathīr, means your people. Were it not for their powerful position over the people of Madyan, they would have stoned him to death. Of the stoning itself he reports two views: some said this means with rocks; it has also been said that they would have cursed and insulted him verbally. Maʿārif states it as the plain threat — had it not been for the support he had from his clan, they would have stoned him to death.

Then: **"and you are not powerful against us."** Ibn Kathīr: "You have no position of power over us." By their reckoning, what stood between the Prophet of Allah and a pile of rocks was his clan's standing, and nothing else.

## Ayah 92: the question that exposes them

They had said he himself was not *ʿazīz* — held no power over them. His reply asks whether his clan is *aʿazz*, of more weight, to them **than Allah**.

Ibn Kathīr renders his meaning: *You would leave me alone out of respect for my people but not out of respect for the greatness of the Lord, the Most Blessed and Exalted? Does not your awe of Allah prevent you from harming His Prophet?* They were not people who feared nothing. A group of men could restrain them; the fear of Allah did not.

**"And you have cast Him behind your backs."** Ibn Kathīr: "you have thrown it behind you. You do not obey it, nor do you respect it." The picture is of something put out of sight, behind the shoulder — not argued with, simply not consulted.

**"Indeed my Lord is surrounding all that you do."** Ibn Kathīr: "This means that He knows all of your actions and He will reward you according to them." Two things, then: a knowledge from which nothing they do escapes, and a requital that follows from it. Their threat had been made in their own town, on their own terms. This is the answer to that.

Maʿārif sums up his bearing here: despite the threat, Shuʿayb, true to his mettle as a prophet, did not hesitate to tell them that they feared his clan all right, but had no fear of Allah, who holds everything in His power.

## Ayah 93: the argument ends, the waiting begins

Ibn Kathīr heads this section *Shuʿayb's threatening of his people*, and introduces it: **when the Prophet of Allah, Shuʿayb, despaired of their response to him**, he said, "O my people…"

**"Act according to your ability"** — Ibn Kathīr: "Act according to your current ways." And then the note that changes how the whole line reads: **"This is actually a severe threat."** It sounds at first like a shrug. It is not. **"I am acting"** — Ibn Kathīr: according to my way. Two roads, and both parties are told simply to keep walking.

**"You will come to know who it is on whom descends the torment that will cover him with ignominy, and who is a liar."** Ibn Kathīr's gloss is brief and settles it: *between me and you*. The matter will not be decided by argument any more. Note too what kind of punishment is promised — one that covers a man with ignominy.

**"And watch! Verily, I too am watching with you."** *Wartaqibū*, says Ibn Kathīr, means to wait. Maʿārif: finally, when his people did not listen to anything said to them, Shuʿayb told them that they could now wait for the punishment.

## Ayah 94: rescue first, then the Cry

**"And when Our commandment came, We saved Shuʿayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us."** Maʿārif calls this the Divine practice: Allah took Shuʿayb and those who had believed in him out of that habitation, and the rest were destroyed. Notice how their rescue is named — *by a mercy from Us*.

**"And the awful Cry seized the wrongdoers, and they lay in their homes."** *Jāthimīn*, says Ibn Kathīr, means extinct and lifeless without any movement. Maʿārif adds that they were destroyed instantly at the harsh Cry of Jibrāʼīl (peace be upon him). The men who had been calculating whether a clan was strong enough to stop them are motionless in the same houses.

## Why *this* punishment here — an observation from Ibn Kathīr

The people of Madyan are described as destroyed differently in different places: here by *aṣ-ṣayḥah*, the awful Cry; in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf by *ar-rajfah*, a severe quake; in Sūrat ash-Shuʿarāʼ by the torment of a cloudy day. Ibn Kathīr's answer is that **they were one nation upon which all of these punishments were gathered on the day of their destruction**, and that in each context Allah mentioned only what was suitable there:

- In al-Aʿrāf they had said, *"We shall certainly drive you out, O Shuʿayb, and those who have believed with you, from our town"* (7:88) — so it was suitable to mention the **quake**: the earth in which they practised their wrongdoing, and from which they wanted to expel their Prophet, shook them.
- **Here**, because of their disrespectful manners in speaking to their Prophet, Allah mentioned the awful **Cry**, which overcame them and killed them.
- In ash-Shuʿarāʼ they had said, *"So cause a piece of the heaven to fall on us, if you are of the truthful"* (26:187) — and Allah said in response, *"So the torment of the day of the Shadow seized them. Indeed that was the torment of a Great Day"* (26:189).

Ibn Kathīr closes with a line worth keeping: "This is from the intricate secrets and to Allah belongs all praise and much bounty forever."

## Ayah 95: erased, and set at a distance

**"As if they had never lived there."** Ibn Kathīr: this means it was as if they had not lived in their homes before that.

**"So away with Madyan, just as Thamūd went away."** Ibn Kathīr explains why Thamūd in particular: they were their **neighbours**, and did not live far from the homes of the people of Madyan. They were similar in their disbelief and in their highway robbery. They were also both Arabs. The comparison, in other words, is to the ruin nearest to them.

## Living it: the sin underneath all of this

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān will not let us forget the concrete crime running through the whole episode. One of the reasons punishment fell on the people of Shuʿayb was their practice of weighing and measuring less than due — *taṭfīf*. The Qur'an describes the severe punishment for it in Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn, which opens: *"Woe to those who give less"* (83:1). There is, Maʿārif states, a consensus of the entire Muslim Ummah that doing so is strictly ḥarām.

Then comes the definition that widens it far beyond the marketplace. Quoting a saying of Sayyidnā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), Imām Mālik has said in the *Muwaṭṭaʼ* that weighing and measuring less essentially means **that someone does not fulfil the right of another person due upon him, fully and duly** — whether it happens to be something given by weight, or by measure, or something of another kind. Maʿārif then applies it:

- an employee who falls short in performing his or her assigned duty;
- an office worker or labourer who cuts his working hours short, or fails to fulfil his job assignment as due;
- and anyone who does not perform his or her Ṣalāh with due consideration of all that is required in it — such a person, Maʿārif says, has also committed the crime of *taṭfīf*.

"May Allah keep all of us protected from it!" Maʿārif adds.

**A related ruling.** Maʿārif cites Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: the people of Shuʿayb would save gold and silver by trimming the edges of the dinar and dirham coins circulating as official currency, then channel those coins back into circulation at par value. Shuʿayb prohibited them from doing so. In Hadith as well, Maʿārif notes, the Prophet ﷺ declared the chipping of the coins of an Islamic state to be ḥarām. The tafsīr authority Zayd ibn Aslam said exactly this in explaining the verse *"nine family heads spreading corruption in the land and not correcting their ways"* (27:48): those people of the city used to chip off gold and silver from dinar and dirham coins and ran a profitable business through it — something the Qur'an calls a great corruption. And from Qurṭubī: during the Khilāfah of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (may Allah have mercy on him), a man was arrested while cutting a dirham coin; he was given a punishment of lashes and paraded around with his head shaved.

## What to carry away

Two sentences from this passage are worth holding on to.

The first is Shuʿayb's question in ayah 92: **"Is my clan of more weight with you than Allah?"** As Ibn Kathīr puts it, they would leave him alone out of respect for his people, but not out of respect for the greatness of their Lord. The question is not whether we fear anything — it is what we fear most, and that is answered by what actually stops us.

The second is the end of the same ayah: **"Indeed my Lord is surrounding all that you do."** Ibn Kathīr's gloss is the whole answer: He knows all of your actions and He will reward you according to them. Ayah 94 is what that came to look like for Madyan — the Cry, and men lifeless in their own homes; and ayah 95, *as if they had never lived there*.

passages.title: Moses, Pharaoh, and a leader into the Fire
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Allah sent Musa (peace be upon him) to Firʿawn and his chiefs with signs and clear proof — and they followed Firʿawn instead. Ayat 96–99 then carry that choice past this world: the man they walked behind here goes in front of them again on the Day of Resurrection, and this time he leads them into the Fire.

The thread holding the four ayat together is one idea: **following**. They followed his command (97), so he goes ahead of them to the Fire (98), and a curse follows them in both worlds (99). Whoever you walk behind here, you walk behind there.

## Where the passage sits

Surah Hud has been moving through nation after nation. Immediately before this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the close of Shuʿayb's story: he warned his people not to let their hostility towards him bring on them what struck the people of Nuh, Hud and Salih, and reminded them that the overturned habitations of Lut's people were near them in place and recent in time. They were enraged, and said that but for the support of his clan they would have stoned him. He answered plainly that they feared his clan but had no fear of Allah, in whose power everything lies. In the end, as is the Divine practice, Allah took out Shuʿayb and those who had believed with him from that habitation, and the rest were destroyed instantly at the harsh Cry of Jibrāʼīl.

Then comes Musa and Firʿawn — and something in the telling reaches further. Shuʿayb's people are followed only to the Cry that ended them. Here the account does not stop with a generation in this world: ayah 98 carries the very same people forward to the Day of Resurrection, still standing in the same order behind the same man.

## Ayah 96: signs, and a proof that is called manifest

Musa is sent, in the words of this passage, "with Our signs and compelling proof" — rendered elsewhere in the same sources as "Our Ayat and a manifest authority." Ibn Kathir puts it in plain prose: in these verses Allah informs of "His sending Musa with His signs and clear proofs to Firʿawn, the king of the Coptic people, and his chiefs."

Notice how the passage opens its own account. Before anything is said about what Egypt did, it is established what Egypt was given: signs, and a proof described as clear and manifest. Nothing in these sources suggests the evidence was thin or the case obscure. Whatever happened next happened in full light.

## Ayah 97: the king and his chiefs

The mission goes "to Firʿawn and his chiefs." The ayah does not name the ruler by himself. His chiefs are named beside him — and the verb that follows is plural: "**but they followed** the command of Firʿawn." A ruler's course became a whole circle's course, and then a people's.

Ibn Kathir will not let that word "command" shrink down to a single order issued on a single day. He glosses it: "they followed his path, way and methodology in transgression." What was followed was a road and a method — a way of running life — not one decree obeyed under duress.

Then the verdict: "**and the command of Firʿawn was no right guide**." Look carefully at what is being weighed here. Not Firʿawn's power, not his standing, not the size of the crowd behind him — the judgement falls on his *amr*, the command or course itself, the thing being followed. Ibn Kathir: "there was no right guidance in it. It was only ignorance, misguidance, disbelief and stubbornness."

And by Ibn Kathir's own description the following was real and complete — "he was their leader and chief." Being genuinely followed, genuinely obeyed, genuinely at the head of a nation did not move the verdict on his command by an inch.

## Ayah 98: the same procession, re-formed at the Fire

Here is the turn the whole passage is built for, and Ibn Kathir states it exactly: "Just as they followed him in this life and he was their leader and chief, likewise he will lead them to the Hellfire on the Day of Resurrection."

Nothing about the arrangement changes. Same leader, same column, same obedience — only the destination is finally visible. "**He will go ahead of his people on the Day of Resurrection, and will lead them into the Fire.**" He is still out in front, where he always was.

Ibn Kathir keeps going, and his own words hold an image of arrival and of drinking: "He will lead them directly to it and they will drink from springs of destruction." They arrive where their leader brings them, and what is there is destruction. The ayah then passes its own comment on the destination: "**and evil indeed is the place to which they are led**."

## The double share: no one escapes on another's account

Ibn Kathir first follows the man at the front: "Firʿawn will have a great share in that awful punishment." He cites Allah's word — "But Firʿawn disobeyed the Messenger; so We seized him with a severe punishment" (73:16) — and the fuller passage: "But Firʿawn belied and disobeyed. Then he turned his back, striving (against Allah). Then he gathered (his people) and cried aloud, saying: 'I am your lord, most high.' So Allah seized him with exemplary punishment for his last and first transgression. Verily, in this is an instructive admonition for whosoever fears Allah" (79:21–26).

*Then he gathered his people and cried aloud.* The verse does not describe a man going wrong quietly by himself. It describes him assembling a crowd and calling out to them — and it closes by naming itself an instructive admonition for whoever fears Allah.

Ibn Kathir then widens it beyond Firʿawn: "This will be the condition of those who were followed. They will have a great share of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection." The one at the head of any column is being described here, not only this one.

But being led is no shelter either. Ibn Kathir sets beside this: "For each one there is double (torment), but you know not" (7:38). And he notes what the disbelievers will say *while they are in the Hellfire*: "Our Lord! Verily, we obeyed our chiefs and our great ones, and they misled us from the (right) way. Our Lord! Give them double torment" (33:67–68).

Read where that sentence is spoken from. "We were only obeying our chiefs" is not an argument made at the gate and accepted; the sources place it on the lips of people already inside. And what Ibn Kathir lays alongside it is not relief for the followers but "for each one there is double." Both the one who set the direction and the one who chose to walk it carry a weight of their own.

## Ayah 99: two curses, and a "gift" called evil

"**They were pursued by a curse in this (deceiving life of this world) and (so they will be pursued by a curse) on the Day of Resurrection, evil indeed is the gift granted.**"

Set the renderings side by side and a reversal comes into view. In ayah 97 they are the ones following — "they followed the command of Firʿawn." In ayah 99 they are the ones followed: Ibn Kathir explains the point of the phrase as, "We have made them to be followed by something more than the punishment of the Fire and that is their being cursed in this life." They chased after a course; now something runs behind them, and it is a curse.
