And note what that tells us about the Fire: it was not the whole of the reckoning. A punishment was added that begins here, in this world, before any of the Hereafter arrives.

On the second half of the ayah the early authorities are gathered:

- **Mujahid**: "Another curse will be added to them on the Day of Resurrection, so these are two curses."
- **Ibn ʿAbbas**, reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah, on "evil indeed is the gift granted": "The curse of this life and the Hereafter."
- **Ad-Dahhak** and **Qatadah** both said the same thing.

Then there is the word the ayah itself chooses. What they receive is called a *gift* — and the gift, on the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas and those who agreed with him, is a curse in this life and in the Hereafter. The ayah's own comment on that gift is the last word: *bi'sa*, "evil indeed."

Ibn Kathir closes with two passages that run in the same order. "And We made them leaders inviting to the Fire: and on the Day of Resurrection, they will not be helped. And We made a curse to follow them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection, they will be among the despised" (28:41–42) — leadership into the Fire, then a curse in this world, then disgrace in the next: exactly the sequence of ayat 97–99. And: "The Fire, they are exposed to it, morning and afternoon. And on the Day when the Hour will be established (it will be said to the angels): 'Cause Firʿawn's people to enter the severest torment!'" (40:46) — an exposure that runs morning and afternoon, and then, when the Hour is established, what is called *the severest*.

## Living it

**Audit what you are following, not only whom.** The ayah passes its verdict on Firʿawn's *command* — his path, way and methodology, in Ibn Kathir's words. That is the thing to examine before you fall in behind anyone: not his standing, not how many are already walking there, but whether the course itself is a right guide. Ibn Kathir's inventory of what Firʿawn's road was actually made of is worth holding up against any road: "ignorance, misguidance, disbelief and stubbornness."

**"We were only obeying" is a sentence spoken inside the Fire.** Ibn Kathir places 33:67–68 in the mouths of people already in Hellfire, and sets 7:38 beside it — "For each one there is double." Anyone who has ever adopted a way of living mainly because the people around them adopted it should sit quietly with where that complaint is being made from.

**If people follow you, this passage is heavier on you, not lighter.** "This will be the condition of those who were followed. They will have a great share of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection." Every parent, teacher, elder, or anyone whose choices set a direction for others is inside that sentence. The verse Ibn Kathir cites does not stop at Firʿawn's disbelief; it records that "he gathered (his people) and cried aloud."

**And the reverse holds.** The weight of ayah 98 is that the arrangement survives death — the one at the front of the line here is still at the front there. So there are two questions worth carrying: whose line am I standing in, and where does the line behind me lead?

passages.title: They wronged only themselves — and the Lord's grip
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These three ayat step back from the individual stories of the earlier nations and look at them together. Ibn Kathir sets the passage up in exactly that way: "When Allah mentioned the story of the Prophets and what happened with them and their nations – how He destroyed the disbelievers and saved the believers – He goes on to say, *That is some of the news of the (population of) towns.*"

Three things follow. These accounts are news that Allah Himself relates to His Prophet ﷺ (ayah 100). The destruction was not an injustice — the people wronged themselves, and the gods they called on added nothing but loss (ayah 101). And the same seizing waits for anyone who is like them (ayah 102).

## The scene these ayat look back on

The story immediately behind them is Madyan and Sayyidna Shuʿayb (peace be upon him). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces how it ended. After counselling his people, Shuʿayb warned them of Allah's punishment: *And O my people, let not your hostility towards me cause you to suffer what was suffered by the people of Nūḥ, or the people of Hūd, or the people of Ṣāliḥ. And the people of Lūṭ are not far from you.*

Maʿārif explains that last sentence in two dimensions at once. The overturned habitations of the people of Sayyidna Lūṭ (peace be upon him) were physically close to Madyan; and in terms of time, the punishment that came upon them was very recent. From this, Maʿārif says, they could learn their lesson and leave their obstinacy. Shuʿayb was not asking them to believe a legend. He was pointing at evidence near them in place and near them in memory.

Their answer was rage. Maʿārif records that they said had it not been for the support he had from his clan, they would have stoned him to death. Despite the threat, Shuʿayb — true to his mettle as a prophet — did not hesitate to tell them that they feared his clan all right, but would have no fear of Allah who holds everything in His power. When nothing said to them landed, he finally told them they could now wait for the punishment. Then, as is the Divine practice, Allah took Shuʿayb and those who had believed with him out of that habitation, and the rest were destroyed instantly at the harsh Cry of Sayyidna Jibrāʾīl (peace be upon him).

That is the scene ayah 100 turns to survey.

## Ayah 100: "some still standing, and some reaped"

Ibn Kathir glosses the two key words precisely. **Qāʾim** — "still standing" — he explains as *still remaining*. **Ḥaṣīd** — rendered "reaped" — he explains as *totally destroyed*.

So the ayah gives two categories, not one. Some sites still remain. Others have been wiped out completely. Both belong to the same body of evidence, caught at different stages — which is why Shuʿayb could point his listeners toward the overturned towns of Lūṭ's people and expect them to understand.

*A reflection, not a claim from the commentaries:* the word chosen for the second category is a harvest word. A reaped field is not described as a catastrophe; it is described as a season that ended.

The other load-bearing phrase in ayah 100 is *naquṣṣuhu ʿalayk* — **"We relate it to you."** The rendering given here is explicit about who is being addressed: *These are accounts, We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺.* Ibn Kathir keeps the sense plain — this is *news of them*, delivered. These are not inherited stories the Prophet ﷺ gathered; they are an account given to him by his Lord.

## Ayah 101: the word that turns three times

Read ayat 101 and 102 together and the same root — **ẓ-l-m**, wronging — sounds three times in the ayat themselves: *mā ẓalamnāhum* (We did not wrong them), *ẓalamū anfusahum* (they wronged themselves), *wa hiya ẓālimah* (while they were doing wrong). The passage is settling where the wrong actually sat.

Ibn Kathir pins each clause down. On *We wronged them not*, he says this means: "when We destroyed them." That is worth pausing on. The denial is not a vague statement about Allah's general kindness to them — it attaches to the act of destruction itself. The very stroke that ended them contained no injustice.

On *but they wronged themselves*, Ibn Kathir specifies what the wrong was: "their rejecting their Messengers and disbelieving in them." Not, in the first instance, the shortchanged scales — the core injury was refusing the messenger Allah had sent to them.

*A reflection:* notice that the Qur'an does not simply say they sinned. It says they wronged **their own souls**. Whatever they thought they were doing to Shuʿayb, or to their customers, the account was posted against themselves.

## The gods that added nothing

Ayah 101 then closes the case on what they had been trusting instead: *So their gods, whom they used to call upon besides Allah, profited them naught when there came the command of your Lord.* Ibn Kathir identifies these as "their idols that they used to worship and invoke," and says flatly that the idols "did not benefit them, nor did they save them when Allah's command came for their destruction."

Then the sting: *nor did they add aught to them but **tatbīb***. Mujahid, Qatadah and others explained this word as **loss** — and Ibn Kathir preserves their reasoning: "because the reason for their destruction and their ruin was that they followed those false gods. Therefore, they were losers in this life and the Hereafter."

That is sharper than it first looks. On this reading, a false god is not merely useless in the emergency, sitting inert while the disaster unfolds. Following it was *the reason for* the ruin. It did not fail to add benefit; it added loss. And the loss is booked in both ledgers — this life *and* the Hereafter — so there was not even a comfortable worldly run to show for it.

*A reflection:* this is close to what Shuʿayb had already put to his people. They feared his clan; they had no fear of Allah, who holds everything in His power. The order of real power was exactly inverted in their minds, and ayah 101 states the result.

## Ayah 102: when your Lord seizes

*Such is the punishment of your Lord when He seizes the (population of) towns while they are doing wrong. Verily, His punishment is painful (and) severe.* The translation given for this ayah renders it as the crushing grip of your Lord when He seizes.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as generalising the whole lesson: "It is as though Allah is saying, 'Just as We have destroyed these wicked generations who rejected their Messengers, We will do the same to any who are like them.'"

Notice what the ayah names as the condition. Not the era, not the nation, not the name — *while they are doing wrong*. The towns are identified by their state. That is what carries these ayat out of ancient history and sets them in front of whoever is reading.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith recorded **in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs**, from Abū Mūsā, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Verily, Allah gives respite to a wrongdoer until He seizes him and he cannot escape."* Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this very ayah: *Such is the punishment of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong.*

The Prophet ﷺ placed the hadith and the ayah side by side, and both turn on the same act of seizing. *A reflection:* the one who is given time has not been let off. He is the one still within reach. This is the answer to the oldest objection a believer feels while watching wrongdoing go unbilled for years — respite is not acquittal.

## Living it: the small subtractions

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out, under these ayat, what the wrongdoing at Madyan actually consisted of — and it is startlingly ordinary. One of the reasons punishment fell on Shuʿayb's people was **taṭfīf**: weighing and measuring less than due. Maʿārif points to Sūrah al-Muṭaffifīn, which opens *Woe to those who give less* (83:1), and notes the consensus of the entire Muslim Ummah that the practice is strictly unlawful.

Then the definition widens in a way that should make every one of us uncomfortable. Quoting a saying of Sayyidnā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), Imam Malik states in the Muwaṭṭaʾ that weighing and measuring less essentially means that someone does not fulfil the right of another person due from him fully and duly — he makes it less — "whether it happens to be something given by weight, or measure, or something of another kind." Maʿārif applies that directly: an employee who falls short in performing his assigned duty, an office worker or a labourer who cuts his working hours short or fails to fulfil his job assignment as due — all are counted in this category. And it goes further: anyone who does not perform his Salah with due consideration of everything obligatory in it "has also committed the crime of this taṭfīf." The commentary breaks off into duʿāʾ: *May Allah keep all of us protected from it!*

Maʿārif adds a related ruling from Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: the people of Shuʿayb would save gold and silver by trimming the edges of the dinar and dirham coins circulating in the country as official currency, then channel them back into circulation at par value — and Shuʿayb prohibited them from doing so. In hadith as well, Maʿārif notes, the Prophet ﷺ declared the chipping of the coins of an Islamic state to be unlawful. The tafsir authority Zayd ibn Aslam explained the "nine family heads spreading corruption in the land" of 27:48 in exactly these terms: men who chipped gold and silver off dinar and dirham coins and ran a profitable business of their own from it — something the Qur'an calls a great corruption. Maʿārif closes with a case from the Khilāfah of Sayyidnā ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (may Allah have mercy on him): a man arrested while cutting a dirham coin was given lashes and paraded around with his head shaved.

*A reflection on why this belongs beside "they wronged themselves":* nobody sets out to become a cautionary ruin. On Maʿārif's reading, the wrongdoing is granular — a sliver off a measure, a shaving off a coin, an hour not really worked, a prayer with its obligations quietly trimmed. Each one feels like a small gain at the moment of doing it. Ayah 101 states what the accounts actually showed.

## What the passage asks of us

**Read ruins as evidence.** Ayah 100 hands over the news deliberately — some sites still remaining, some totally destroyed — and Maʿārif shows Shuʿayb asking his people to reason from exactly this kind of evidence, near them in place and in time.

**Audit what you are leaning on.** Ayah 101 does not say the idols were merely worthless. On Mujahid and Qatadah's reading, following them was the reason for the ruin, and the loss ran into both worlds.

**Do not misread the delay.** The hadith of Abū Mūsā in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, and the ayah the Prophet ﷺ recited alongside it, together say that time given to a wrongdoer is time, not clemency.

And one thing more, especially for anyone carrying a hard message to people who do not want it. The account is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself: *We relate it to you.* Allah tells him that He destroyed the deniers and saved the believers, that the record is His own, and that nothing in it was unjust. Ibn Kathir's summary — "We will do the same to any who are like them" — is a warning to the obstinate. *A reflection:* to the one being threatened for telling the truth, as Shuʿayb was, it is also a steadying word.

passages.title: The Gathering Day and the two destinies
passages.tafsir:
**Before these verses, Surah Hud has been walking through the destruction of the towns.** Ibn Kathir titles his commentary here exactly that: *The Destruction of the Towns is a Proof of the Establishment of the Hour.* The passage immediately preceding belongs to Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) and his people. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recounts that earlier narrative, Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) warned his people not to let their hostility toward him bring down on them what had already come upon the people of Nuh, or of Hud, or of Salih — and reminded them that the overturned habitations of the people of Lut (peace be upon them all) were close by, near Madyan, and recent in time, so they could learn the lesson and give up their obstinacy. His people were enraged and said that were it not for the support of his clan they would have stoned him. He answered that they feared his clan but had no fear of Allah, who holds everything in His power. Finally, when they would not listen, he told them to wait for the punishment. Then, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, "as is the Divine practice," Allah brought Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) and those who had believed with him out of that habitation, and the rest were destroyed instantly at the harsh Cry of Jibra'il (peace be upon him).

Ayah 103 stands at the edge of those ruins and says: look carefully — there is a sign here. From that sign the passage moves forward to the Day those ruins were rehearsing, and then to the only two destinations that Day produces. Ayat 103–108 are one movement: from history's small judgements to the final one, and from the final one to two homes that never end.

## The sign in the ruins (103)

Ibn Kathir explains the opening exactly this way. When Allah says **"Indeed in that (there) is a sure lesson,"** He means: in Our destroying the disbelievers and Our saving the believers. That double outcome is "an admonition and lesson concerning the truthfulness of that which We are promised in the Hereafter." History has already shown, in miniature, that Allah does separate people and does keep His word. He supports this with His statement, *"Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in this world's life and on the Day when the witnesses will stand forth"* (40:51), and with *"So their Lord revealed to them: Truly, We shall destroy the wrongdoers"* (14:13).

Notice who the sign is for: **"for those who fear the torment of the Hereafter."** The ruins are visible to everyone; what they *mean* opens to a heart that already takes the Hereafter seriously.

## Two descriptions of one Day (103)

The ayah then gives that Day two descriptions, and each says something the other does not.

**"That is a Day whereon mankind will be gathered together."** Ibn Kathir glosses it: "the first of them and the last of them," and cites *"And We shall gather them all together so as to leave not one of them behind"* (18:47). Not a sample. Not a generation. Everyone, from the first to the last, with no exemptions and no absentees.

**"and that is a Day when all will be present."** Ibn Kathir says this means "a day that is great," and then fills the scene in: the angels will be present, the Messengers will gather, and all of creation will be gathered with their families — "the humans, Jinns, birds, wild beasts and domesticated riding animals will all be gathered." Every creature that ever drew breath is in the crowd.

And then the single most reassuring line in his commentary on this ayah: **"Then the Most Just, Who does not wrong anyone even an atom's weight, will judge between them and He will increase their good deeds in reward."** The gathering is not a mob scene; it is a court, and the Judge neither shaves an atom off what you are owed nor charges you an atom you did not earn — and He gives *more* than the deed deserves.

## "For a term already fixed" (104)

**"And We delay it only for a term (already) fixed."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is one sentence, and it closes off both directions at once: "a fixed period of time that cannot be increased or decreased."

So the delay is not indecision, and it is not weakness. It is an appointment already set. Nothing anyone does brings it forward; nothing anyone does pushes it back.

## The silence of that Day (105)

**"On the Day when it comes, no person shall speak except by His (Allah's) leave."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is plain: on the Day of Judgement no one will speak except with the permission of Allah. He gathers the parallels — *"they will not speak except him whom the Most Gracious allows, and he will speak what is right"* (78:38), and *"And all the voices will be humbled for the Most Gracious"* (20:108).

Then he brings the hadith about the intercession, **recorded in the Two Sahihs**, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"No one will speak on that day except the Messengers, and the call of the Messengers will be, 'O Allah, save us, save us.'"*

Sit with that. On the Day when the mouths of all creation are sealed shut, the only ones given leave to speak are the Messengers — and what they say is not a claim, not a defence, not a résumé. It is a plea repeated twice: save us, save us. If that is the speech of the best of creation on that Day, the confidence we carry about our own standing needs revisiting tonight, not then.

## Wretched and blessed — and 'Umar's question (105)

The verse ends by sorting the entire gathering into two words: **"Some among them will be wretched and (others) blessed."** Ibn Kathir: of the people of the gathering, "some will be miserable and some will be happy," as Allah said, *"When a party will be in Paradise and a party in the blazing Fire"* (42:7). There is no third column, no unclassified remainder. Every person in that immense crowd falls under one of two headings.

Al-Hafiz Abu Yaʿla recorded in his *Musnad*, on the authority of Ibn 'Umar, that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: when this verse was revealed — *"Some among them will be wretched and (others) blessed"* — he asked the Prophet ﷺ, "O Messenger of Allah, will there be a sign for us to know (which party we are from)? Will it be because of something that a person did, or something that he did not do?" He answered:

> *"O 'Umar, it will be due to something that he did and the pens wrote it down. But every easy deed was created for its purpose (to be carried out)."*

Read the answer slowly. It holds two things together without letting go of either: the pens have already written, *and* the outcome is tied to something the person actually does. 'Umar asked for a sign he could read in advance; he was answered with deeds. That is the only sign the report gives us, and it is enough to be going on with.

## The Fire: two kinds of breathing (106)

**"As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, in it they will experience Zafir and Shahiq."** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas: "*Az-Zafir* is a sound in the throat and *Ash-Shahiq* is a sound in the chest. This means that their exhaling will be *Zafir* and their inhaling will be *Shahiq*." Ibn Kathir adds that this will be due to the torment they will be experiencing — the two halves of a single breath, both of them turned into groaning. Then he breaks off his own commentary to say: "We seek refuge with Allah from such evil." Even breathing, the one act a living body does without thinking, becomes suffering.

## "As long as the heavens and the earth endure" (107, 108)

Both destinies are then described with the same phrase — the Fire in ayah 107, the Garden in ayah 108: **"abiding therein for all the time that the heavens and the earth endure."**

Imam Abu Jaʿfar bin Jarir explains it first as Arab idiom. When the Arabs wanted to describe something that would last forever they would say, "This is as enduring as the heavens and the earth," or "It will last until the night and day separate," or "As long as talkers at night continue to chat." They meant, by all of these, the condition of eternity. "Therefore," he says, "Allah addressed them in a manner that they were familiar with among themselves."

But Ibn Kathir adds that the literal meaning is intended too — because there will *be* heavens and earth in the life of the next world, as Allah said, *"On the Day when the earth will be changed to another earth and so will be the heavens"* (14:48). For this reason Al-Hasan Al-Basri said: "Allah is referring to a heaven other than this heaven and an earth other than this earth. That new heaven and earth will be eternal." So the measure is not the sky we see now; it is the sky of the world that never ends.

## The exception — "except as your Lord wills"

Each of the two verses carries the same clause: **"except as your Lord wills."** Ibn Kathir shows that this exception does different work in each place.

**On the side of the Fire (107),** he pairs it with *"The Fire be your dwelling place, you will dwell therein forever, except as Allah may will. Certainly your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing"* (6:128). He then reports: "It has been said that the exception mentioned in this verse refers to the disobedient among the people of *Tawhid*" — that is, believers in Allah's oneness who fell into disobedience. These are the ones Allah will bring out of the Fire "by the intercession of the interceders," and he names who those interceders are: the angels, the Prophets and the believers. They will intercede "even on behalf of those who committed major sins." Then, he says, "the generous mercy of Allah will remove from the Fire those who have never done any good, except for saying *La ilaha illallah* one day of their life." He states that this has been mentioned in numerous authentic reports from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, including narrations from Anas bin Malik, Jabir bin 'Abdullah, Abu Saʿid Al-Khudri, Abu Hurayrah and other Companions. And he closes the door carefully: "No one remains in the Fire after this final intercession, except those who will remain there forever without escape." Ibn Kathir presents this as "the opinion held by many of the scholars, both past and present, concerning the explanation of this verse" — a widely held reading, reported as such rather than as the only possible one.

**On the side of the Garden (108),** the same clause is read differently. Ibn Kathir first identifies who these people are: **"And those who are blessed"** — "these are the followers of the Messengers"; **"they will be in Paradise"** — "this means that their final abode will be Paradise"; **"abiding therein for all the time"** — "this means that they will remain there forever." Then, on the exception: its meaning is "that the condition of eternal pleasure that they will experience therein is something that is not mandatory by itself. Rather, it is something that is dependent upon the will of Allah. Unto Him belongs the favour of immortality upon them." Nobody has a *claim* on Paradise that runs on its own; it continues because Allah continues it. And he adds a line worth carrying: "For this reason they are inspired to glorify and praise Him, just as they are inspired to breathe." In Paradise, praise is not a duty imposed from outside — it is as natural and as constant as breath. Set that against ayah 106, where the wretched *also* breathe endlessly, and their breathing is groaning. Two eternities, two kinds of breath.

Ibn Kathir also reports a second view of the exception in ayah 108: Ad-Dahhak and Al-Hasan Al-Basri both said, "It is about the right of the disobedient people of Tawhid who were in the Fire and then brought out of it" — that is, the exception marks those who reach the Garden late, after being brought out.

## "A gift without an end" (108)

The passage's last words are **"a gift without an end."** Ibn Kathir: "This means that it will never be cut off," reporting this from Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Al-'Aliyah and others.

He explains exactly why the phrase is placed here: it is mentioned "so that the suspicious person will not doubt after the mention of the will of Allah. Someone may think that the mention of Allah's will here means that the pleasure of Paradise may end or change. To the contrary, it has been decreed that this pleasure will truly be forever and will never end." The exception clause was there to teach you that Paradise is dependent on Allah's will; the closing phrase is there so you never mistake that dependence for insecurity. Ibn Kathir's own words: "Here, Allah soothes the hearts and affirms the intent."

He notes the other side too: Allah has clarified that the eternal torment of the people of the Fire is likewise due to His will, and that He punishes them "due to His justness and wisdom." Which is why the verse says, **"Verily, your Lord is the doer of whatsoever He intends."** Ibn Kathir sets beside it: *"He cannot be questioned as to what He does, while they will be questioned"* (21:23).

## From the Sunnah: the day death dies

Ibn Kathir seals the passage with two reports. **Recorded in the Two Sahihs**, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"Death will be brought in the form of a handsome ram (on the Day of Judgement) and it will be slaughtered between Paradise and the Hellfire. Then, it will be said: 'O people of Paradise! Eternity and no death! O people of Hellfire! Eternity and no death!'"*

And **in the Sahih** it is recorded that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"It will be said: 'O people of Paradise, verily you will live and you will never die. You will remain young and you will never grow old. You will remain healthy and you will never become ill. You will be happy and you will never grieve.'"*

Every fear that shadows human happiness in this world — dying, ageing, falling ill, losing what you love — is named and cancelled, one by one. That is what "a gift without an end" means in plain experience.

## Living it

**Read the ruins.** Ayah 103 says the lesson is for "those who fear the torment of the Hereafter," and Ibn Kathir says the lesson is in the destroying of the disbelievers and the saving of the believers together. The evidence is public; the eyesight is not. Cultivate the seriousness that makes history legible.

**Do not misread the delay.** Ayah 104: the term is fixed, and "cannot be increased or decreased." That the Day has not come is not evidence that it is not coming.

**Prepare your case now, because you may not get to plead it.** Ayah 105 shows a Day of sealed mouths, where even the Messengers say only *"O Allah, save us, save us."* Whatever you would want to explain on that Day, fix it in this one.

**Stop looking for a sign and look at your deeds.** That was the Prophet's ﷺ answer to 'Umar. He was not handed a label to read in advance; he was answered with what a person does.

**Hold fear and hope in the same hand.** The same passage that describes breathing turned to groaning also records that Allah's generous mercy reaches a person who never did any good beyond saying *La ilaha illallah* one day of his life. That is not a licence — those brought out are brought out *of the Fire*, after entering it. It is a reason never to despair of Allah, and never to gamble on Him.

**And say what they say in the Garden.** Ibn Kathir says the people of Paradise are inspired to glorify and praise Allah just as they are inspired to breathe. That habit does not begin there. It begins with a tongue that is already used to it.

passages.title: Inherited worship, disputed scripture, full recompense
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat speak directly to the Prophet ﷺ, and they say three things at once: the idolatry in front of him has no argument behind it, disagreement over revelation is an old story he need not take personally, and the delay in judgement changes nothing about the final settlement — everyone will be paid in full.

What holds the passage together is a single image: **exact, undiminished payment**. Ayah 109 promises a portion delivered "without diminution"; ayah 111 states that every soul's works will be repaid in full. Between them, in ayah 110, sits the reason nothing has been settled yet.

## "So be not in doubt"

Ayah 109 opens with an address to the Prophet ﷺ: "So be not in doubt as to what these people worship." Ibn Kathir explains that "this refers to the polytheists," and that the command carries a verdict on what they are doing: "what they are doing is falsehood, ignorance and misguidance."

It is worth being clear about what the Prophet ﷺ is being steadied against. A messenger surrounded by a confident, ancient, socially respectable religion — practised by the fathers and handed down unquestioned — is being told that its confidence is not evidence. Numbers and antiquity look like proof. They are not. The verse settles the question before the doubt has anywhere to stand.

## A religion inherited, never examined

The second half of ayah 109 gives the reason the doubt is baseless: "They worship nothing but what their fathers worshipped before them." Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion sharply — they "have no support for their Shirk. They are only mimicking their fathers in ignorance." (*Shirk* is associating partners with Allah, directing to another what belongs to Him alone.)

This is the whole case for their religion, and the Qur'an states it as an indictment rather than a defence. There is no revelation behind it, no argument, no evidence they could produce if pressed — only the fact that this is how it has always been done here. Notice that the verse does not accuse them of having examined the truth and rejected it; it describes them as mimicking. Ibn Kathir calls it mimicry *in ignorance*, and that is a heavier charge than it first sounds: they did not know, and they did not need to know, because inheritance did the thinking for them.

The application to a believer is uncomfortable and worth sitting with. Inherited religion is not automatically wrong — family is how most people first meet the truth. What the ayah condemns is inheritance offered *as the reason*: doing something because it is what our people do, with no willingness to ask whether Allah commanded it. A practice does not become sound by being old, and a custom does not become worship by being sincere. The question the ayah presses on every generation is simply: on what authority?

## "Their portion, without diminution"

Ayah 109 closes: "And verily, We shall repay them in full their portion without diminution." Ibn Kathir reports from 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam that this means: "We will pay them in full their portion of punishment without diminution." Ibn Kathir has already said that Allah "will give them due recompense for that and He will punish them with a punishment the likes of which none can give besides Him."

Nothing is left out of that reckoning, and nothing is quietly shaved off it. What is due arrives entire.

Ibn Kathir adds a striking note about the other side of the ledger: "If they did any good deeds, then Allah will reward them for those good works in this life, before the life of the Hereafter." A disbeliever's kindness, generosity, or fair dealing is not simply erased; it is compensated in the currency of this world, and that account is settled here. Nothing is stolen from anyone. Everything is paid where it is payable.

## Musa (peace be upon him) was given the Book, and they differed over it

Ayah 110 opens a window onto a much older scene: "Indeed, We gave the Book to Musa, but differences arose therein." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah "gave Musa the Book, but the people differed concerning it. Some believed in it and some disbelieved in it." Then he states the purpose of the reminder plainly: "Therefore, you, Muhammad, have an example in the Prophets who came before you. So do not grieve or be upset by their denial of you."

This is consolation, and it works by widening the frame. The Prophet ﷺ was watching a divinely given message be argued over and rejected by the very people it came to. The verse tells him: this is what happened to the great scripture before yours, given to one of the great Messengers before you. Rejection is not a sign that the message failed or that the messenger mishandled it.

The ayah itself ends by describing those who reject him now: "and indeed they are in grave doubt concerning it (this Qur'an)." The doubt forbidden to the one carrying the truth is the very condition of those refusing it.

## The Word that went before

The heart of ayah 110 is the conditional: "and had it not been for a Word (*Kalimah*) that had gone forth before from your Lord, the case would have been judged between them." In other words, the only reason the dispute is still running — the only reason the deniers were still walking about arguing — is a prior divine decision.

Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Jarir: "If it were not that the punishment had already been delayed until an appointed time, then Allah would have decided the matter between you now. The word Kalimah carries the meaning that Allah will not punish anyone until the proof has been established against him and a Messenger has been sent to him."

That is a principle of enormous consequence, and Ibn Kathir grounds it in the Qur'an itself — "And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger (to give warning)" (17:15). No one is condemned for missing a message never delivered. Allah binds His own dealing with creation to a standard of established proof that no human court reliably meets.

The pastoral edge of this comes in the second verse Ibn Kathir quotes: "And had it not been for a Word that went forth before from your Lord, and a term determined, (their punishment) must necessarily have come (in this world). **So bear patiently what they say**" (20:129–130). The command that follows the delay is patience. If Allah is holding back judgement until an appointed term, then the believer who is being mocked, denied, or wronged is being asked to hold with Him — not to demand that the ledger be balanced on his own timetable.

Read this way, the delay you experience as injustice is the same mercy that once gave your own life room to change. Judgement withheld is not judgement cancelled; it is time, and time is a gift before it is a reprieve.

## Every last one, repaid in full

Ayah 111 gathers everything up: "And verily, to each of them your Lord will repay their works in full. Surely, He is All-Aware of what they do."

Ibn Kathir writes: "Then, Allah informs that He will gather the early generations and the later generations from all of the nations. He will then reward them based upon their deeds. If they did good deeds, their reward will be good, and if they did evil deeds, their reward will be bad." "Each" takes in the deniers standing in front of the Prophet ﷺ, the ones who believed Musa (peace be upon him) and the ones who did not, and everyone reading this now. Ibn Kathir supports it with "And surely, all — everyone of them will be brought before Us" (36:32).

Then the closing name: **al-Khabir**, "All-Aware." Ibn Kathir unpacks it: "He is All-Knower of all of their deeds. This includes their honorable deeds and their despicable deeds, their small deeds and their great deeds." A judge who missed the small acts could not pay in full. Nothing done in private is outside the file, and nothing is small enough to be forgotten. We affirm this attribute as Allah has described Himself, without likening His knowledge to ours and without emptying the word of its meaning.

Ibn Kathir also notes that "there are many different modes of recitation for this verse, yet all of their meanings agree with what we have mentioned." In a passage about a scripture that people fell into disagreement over, that is worth pausing on: the transmitted variation here does not pull the meaning apart.

**The passage in one line:** their religion has no case, your grief has no cause, the delay has a reason, and the account will be settled in full by One who missed nothing.

passages.title: Stand firm, shun wrongdoers, pray and endure
passages.tafsir:
Surah Hud has spent most of its length on the ruined towns — prophets who warned, peoples who refused — some still standing as ruins, others erased like harvested fields (ayah 100). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that once these events end, it is by addressing the Prophet ﷺ that the whole community is exhorted to draw its lessons. These four ayat are that instruction, one chain: **stand firm — do not tilt toward the wrongdoers — establish the prayer — endure** — closing with a promise that none of it is wasted.

## The ayah that made the Prophet ﷺ grow old

Ibn ʿAbbas said that of everything revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, no ayah was harder or more trying than ayah 112. Maʿārif preserves the scene: the Companions, noticing some grey strands in his blessed beard, remarked that old age was approaching him much earlier. He said, **"Surah Hud has made me old."**

Ibn ʿAbbas said that this ayah alone was the reason. Tafsir al-Qurtubi, as Maʿārif relates, reports from Abu ʿAli Sirriy that he saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream and asked whether Surah Hud had made him old. He said yes. Asked whether it was the punishments that came upon the peoples of the past prophets, he said no — it was *fastaqim kamā umirt*, "So, stand firm — as you have been commanded."

Maʿārif offers two possibilities without choosing. Perhaps because the ayah does not ask for firmness in an absolute sense; it asks that the standing firm be **as Allah commanded** — so that despite his perfect firmness he was still concerned whether he had come up to the rectitude his Master expected. And it is also possible that the concern was not for himself at all: the command in this ayah was given to the entire Ummah too, and it was his realisation that his Ummah may find it difficult to stand firm as commanded that made him sad.

Maʿārif also notes a pattern in how the passage is addressed: the positive commands go to the Prophet ﷺ with the community included as a corollary, while the prohibitions are beamed at the community directly — an indication of his high station, since the things worth leaving off are things he himself abstained from.

## Istiqāmah: standing straight

**Istiqāmah** means to stand straight without the least tilt one way or the other. Maʿārif makes the difficulty vivid: expert engineers can set a vertical object of iron or rock perfectly upright at the very outset. To have a *moving* object stand straight at all times and under all conditions is something else entirely.

Its reach is wide: to move straight, as commanded by Allah, within the limits He set — in beliefs, acts of worship, personal and collective transactions, morals, social dealings, and economic pursuits. If the slightest tilt, shortcoming or excess occurs in any of those, istiqāmah is the first casualty.

Maʿārif traces the errors around us to this deviation. When people do not stand firm in **beliefs**, they start with self-invented practices in religion (bidʿah) and end in the extremes of kufr and shirk. What the Prophet ﷺ conveyed of Allah's Oneness, His Being and His Attributes is moderate and sound; those who commit any excess or deficiency in it — even with good intentions — are astray and in error. The tilt runs both ways with the prophets: those who belittle the honour and love due to them are astray and audacious, and those who commit the excess of assigning a prophet proprietary rights in Divine attributes and powers cross those limits just as surely — an error, Maʿārif notes, that the Jews and the Christians lost themselves in. The same holds in **worship**: the methods determined by the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ are great benchmarks, and any slicing or undercutting of them drags a person down from standing firm, while any addition from one's own side ruins it another way — the tragedy being that such a person honestly thinks he is pleasing Allah when this is precisely the cause of His displeasure. Hence Maʿārif's practical rule: before doing something as an act of worship, one must first find out whether it stands proved from the Prophet ﷺ and his noble Companions in the same state and form. If it does not, let him not waste his time and energy on it.

And the same in **conduct**. Maʿārif describes the Prophet's ﷺ practical teaching as a moderate and sound way of conducting our lives, giving Muslims a straight middle course in friendship and enmity, softness and strictness, miserliness and generosity, economic activity and monasticism, trust in Allah and use of possible material means.

**From the Prophet ﷺ.** Sufyan ibn ʿAbdullah al-Thaqafi asked him for something so comprehensive about Islam that he would need to ask no one after him. He said: *"Say: I believe in Allah. Then, stand firm on it."* (Reported by Muslim, as quoted by al-Qurtubi.)

**From the Companions.** Here the report is an *athar*, a saying of the early generations rather than Prophetic Sunnah. ʿUthman ibn ʿAbdullah al-Azdi went to Ibn ʿAbbas and asked him for some words of advice. He told him to make the fear of Allah essential for himself and to stand firm — *follow, and do not innovate* (reported by al-Darimi in his Musnad, as quoted by al-Qurtubi).

The Sufi authorities have said that standing firm is a station much superior to the working of miracles (karāmah) — meaning that a person holding on firmly to the assignments of his religion is a saint in his own right, even though no miracle ever issued from him.

## "Those who repented with you" — and "do not cross the limits"

The command is given to the Prophet ﷺ *and those who have repented with him* — those who had come out of kufr and stood at his side. Ibn Kathir reads it as Allah commanding His Messenger and His believing servants to be firm and always upright, adding: this **is of the greatest aid for gaining victory over the enemy and confronting the opposition.**

Then *wa lā taṭghaw*. The word derives from **ṭughyān** — to cross limits — which is the opposite of standing firm. Maʿārif notes that the negative had to be clarified expressly, because crossing the limits set by Allah and His Messenger ﷺ is the outlet of all disorder and corruption in material and religious life. Ibn Kathir defines transgression as exceeding the bounds of what is allowed, and warns that it causes destruction to its practitioner — **even if the transgression was directed against a polytheist.** The ayah closes: *He is All-Seer of what you do* — He is not unaware of anything, says Ibn Kathir.

## Ayah 113: the smallest tilt

*And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire should touch you.*

**Rukūn**, Maʿārif explains, means a slight tilt towards one side, having confidence in it and approval of it. Whoever indulges in injustice ruins his life, worldly and spiritual both — but the slightest tilt toward the unjust could also push a person to the edges of the same abyss.

Ibn Kathir gathers the early readings. ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah reported Ibn ʿAbbas as saying it means "Do not compromise with them"; Ibn Jarir reported him as saying "Do not side with those who do wrong" — which Ibn Kathir calls a good statement, glossing it: do not seek assistance from wrongdoers, **because it will be as if you are condoning their actions.**

Maʿārif lines up the rest, noting no contradiction in these statements of the Companions and the Successors:

- **Qatadah:** do not have friendship with the unjust, and do not follow what they say.
- **Ibn Jurayj:** do not nurse a leaning of any kind towards the unjust.
- **Abu al-ʿAliyah:** do not like everything they do.
- **al-Suddiyy:** do not court the favour of the unjust through servile flattery (*mudāhanah*) — that is, do not observe silence or show approval at their evil deeds.
- **ʿIkrimah:** do not sit in the company of the unjust.
- **Qadi al-Baydawi:** following them in personal looks, fashion and ways of living is all included under this same prohibition.

Baydawi also said that this ayah exudes the highest imaginable degree of severity in the matter of injustice. Imam ʿAbdur-Rahman ibn ʿAmr al-Awzaʿi said that with Allah no one is as detested as the scholar who, for the sake of his worldly interest, goes to meet someone unjust (Mazhari). According to Tafsir al-Qurtubi, this ayah tells us it is obligatory (wājib) to abstain from the company of those who disbelieve, those who disobey, and those who innovate in the established religion — **unless they have to be met under some compulsion.**

*You will have no protectors besides Allah, nor will you be helped.* Ibn Kathir: you will not have besides Allah any friend who can save you, nor any helper who can remove you from His torment.

**Hasan al-Basri's summary.** He said that Allah has compressed the entire religion within two occurrences of the word *lā* ("do not") — *lā taṭghaw* in 112 and *lā tarkanū* in 113: the first prohibits crossing the limits set by the Shariʿah, the second the company of wrongdoing people. Company and social setting, Maʿārif adds, play a major role in one's betterment or corruption.

## Ayah 114: and the answer is prayer

*And establish the prayer at both ends of the day, and in the approaches of the night.*

**The timings.** There is a consensus among the early commentators that the prayer at the first end of the day is Fajr. On the other end they differ: Ibn ʿAbbas (via ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah), al-Hasan and ʿAbdur-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam took it as Maghrib; in one narration reported by Qatadah, al-Dahhak and others, al-Hasan said it is ʿAsr — that being the last prayer *of the day*, since the time of Maghrib is not part of the day; Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi and al-Dahhak (in one narration) read it as Fajr at the beginning with Zuhr and ʿAsr at the end.

*Zulafan* is the plural of **zulfah** — the approaches of the night. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and others said this means ʿIsha; al-Hasan is also reported (through Ibn al-Mubarak from Mubarak ibn Fadalah) as saying Maghrib and ʿIsha, and Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ saying that these two are the approaches of the night. Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said the same — the position of the majority of early commentators, per Maʿārif. Read that way, four of the five prayers are named here; Zuhr comes in *"Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun"* (17:78).

**A chronological note.** Ibn Kathir observes that this ayah was revealed before the five daily prayers were made obligatory during the night of Israʾ, when there were only two obligatory prayers: one before sunrise and one before sunset.

**What "establish" means.** Maʿārif reports three positions on *iqāmat al-salāh* — establishing and implementing it fully and faithfully with constant regularity; performing it with due consideration of all its rules of etiquette; performing it at its most preferred time — and concludes there is not much difference between them.

## "Surely good deeds erase bad deeds"

**How this was revealed.** Al-Bukhari recorded Ibn Masʿud saying that a man kissed a woman who was not his relative or wife, then came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him — and this ayah was revealed. The man asked, "O Messenger of Allah, is this only for me?" The Prophet ﷺ replied, *"This is for all of my (Ummah) followers."*

Imam Ahmad recorded a fuller version from Ibn ʿAbbas, in which the man went first to ʿUmar, then to Abu Bakr, before reaching the Prophet ﷺ; there it is ʿUmar who insists the ayah is for people in general, and the Prophet ﷺ confirms: *"ʿUmar has spoken the truth."*

Sit with the shape of that: a man crushed by what he has done is handed not a lecture but a prayer time — and told the mercy is not carved out for him alone.

**What the reports add.** Ibn Kathir gathers several here:

- In the Two Sahihs it is recorded that ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan made wuduʾ for the people to see, just like the wuduʾ of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he ﷺ said: *"Whoever makes Wuduʾ like this Wuduʾ of mine, then he prays two units of prayer in which he does not speak to himself, he will be forgiven for his previous sins."* Maʿārif names this prayer **Salāt al-Tawbah**, reporting it in the Musnad of Ahmad from Abu Bakr, and calls such reports the preferred method of repenting from a sin.
- In the Sahih it is recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Do you think that if there was a flowing river at the door of anyone of you and he bathed in it five times every day, would there be any dirt left on him?"* They said, "No, O Messenger of Allah!" He ﷺ said: *"This is like the five daily prayers, for Allah uses them to wipe away the sins and wrongdoings."*
- Muslim recorded in his Sahih that Abu Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: *"The five daily prayers, Jumuʿah to Jumuʿah and (the fast of) Ramadan to Ramadan are expiations for whatever sins were committed between them, as long as you stay away from the major sins."*

**How far this extends.** *Al-hasanāt*, the early commentators said, means all good deeds — prayer, fasting, zakah, charity, good morals, good dealings — with prayer taking precedence over all of them. *Al-sayyiʾāt* in its wording covers all bad deeds, major or minor, but another ayah and several sayings of the Prophet ﷺ particularise it to minor sins: *"If you abstain from the major [sins] out of what you have been forbidden from, We shall write off your minor sins"* (4:31), and the closing condition in Muslim's report above. Major sins, then, are not forgiven without repentance (tawbah); minor ones do get forgiven as a person keeps doing good deeds. And even then, Maʿārif cites Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit reporting from the authentic scholars of the Principles of the Shariʿah that minor sins are forgiven by good deeds **only when the person feels ashamed of having done them and makes a solemn resolve not to do them in future.**

Maʿārif also relates, with reference to the Musnad of Ahmad through Ibn Kathir, the Prophet's ﷺ words that after a bad deed has been committed, do a good one and it will erase its evil.

**"That is a reminder for the mindful."** Maʿārif notes that *dhālika* could refer to the Qur'an itself, or to the do's and don'ts mentioned earlier. Either way, they are guidance for those who listen to it and are used to obeying it — the hint being that a person so compulsively obstinate that he will not think about anything reasonable remains deprived of every guidance.

## Ayah 115: and be patient

**Sabr** literally means *to tie*. In usage it carries the sense of keeping one's unruly self in control — and included in it, as Maʿārif puts it, is the effort to keep oneself firm in doing what is good and right, as much as the effort to check and hold oneself back from bad deeds.

Patient with what? Maʿārif allows both readings: the injunctions just given him are things he should hold fast to; and it is also possible that the purpose is patience in the face of the hostility of enemies and the pains they cause.

Then the promise: *Allah lets not the reward of the good-doers be lost.* Maʿārif reads *al-muhsinīn* straight out of the passage: they are the people who faithfully observe the do's and don'ts given in these ayat.

Behind all of it, Maʿārif says, is the Prophet's ﷺ own definition of **ihsān**: to obey and worship Allah as though you are seeing Him, or at the least, that Allah is seeing you. When a person reaches that station of certitude about Allah's Being and Attributes, all words and deeds that issue from him become correct of their own accord.

Maʿārif closes with three sayings so well recognised among the early scholars that they used to exchange them in writing (from Tafsir Ruh al-Bayan): whoever gets busy working for the Hereafter, Allah takes it upon Himself to put his worldly affairs in order; whoever corrects his inward state, turning his heart away from everything and toward Allah, has his outward state corrected all by itself; and whoever puts his matter with Allah right, Allah Himself sets right all matters pertaining to him and to those he deals with.

## Living it

*The commentaries end here. What follows is one reader's attempt to put the passage to work — not a report from any of them.*

Audit yourself for tilt rather than collapse: on Maʿārif's reading, istiqāmah is lost not only by abandoning religion but by the slightest excess or shortfall in belief, worship, money, temper or dealings. Watch not only who your enemies are but whose approval you court, whose silence you keep, whose manner you copy — that is the ground the commentators cover under *rukūn*. Guard the prayer where the passage places it, since it appears here not as a duty stacked on top of the struggle but as the answer given to it. When you fall, make wuduʾ and pray — then keep going, on the promise that no reward of the doers of good is lost. And notice the frame: it opens by telling you *He is All-Seer of what you do*, and ends by naming the people who live as though they know it. And Allah knows best.

passages.title: Why nations fall and why people differ
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These four ayat look back at "the generations before you" — the peoples who were destroyed — and answer two questions about them: *why* did those societies actually fall, and, if the truth was so plain, why do human beings still not agree about it?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the first half plainly: ayat 116 and 117 give the reason why divine punishment came upon past peoples, along with the instruction as to how they could have stayed safe from it. Ayat 118–119 then turn to the second question: why people differ, and who is excepted from the blame.

## Ayah 116: the people who were not there

The ayah does not open by listing the sins of the ruined nations. It opens with a lament about the good people who should have existed and did not: *If only there had been among the generations before you persons having wisdom, prohibiting others from corruption in the earth.*

Ibn Kathir reads it as a statement that there *should* have been a group of wise people present among those past generations — people who called to good and forbade the evil and corruption taking place around them in the land. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches the tone exactly: how sad that among them there could have been at least *some* good and wise people who would have stopped their erring fellow-men from spreading disorder.

**The word that carries the ayah: baqiyyah.** The Qurʼān calls these missing people ʾūlū baqiyyah — literally "possessors of a remnant". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *baqiyyah* means *that which remains*, and identifies the people so described as people of discernment, balance and foresight. Then it gives a beautiful reason for the choice of word. It is human habit that a person lets what is most dear to him remain with him under all conditions, preserved and retrievable; when some need arises, he will give away everything but not that. So reason and insight are themselves called a man's *baqiyyah* — his remnant — because that is the dearest thing he has.

Read that back into the ayah and it stings. What was missing was not a rare gift. It was the one thing a person is supposed to hold back and never spend.

**"Except a few."** Ibn Kathir notes that the exception in the ayah — *illā qalīlan mimman anjaynā minhum* — means that there were only a small number of people among them who were of this calibre, and that those were the ones Allah saved at the sudden striking of His vengeance, when His anger was let loose. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: the exception was a counted few who followed the noble prophets, and they were the ones who stayed safe from the punishment.

Hold those two facts together, because both tafsirs put them side by side: the ones who forbade the corruption are precisely the ones Allah rescued.

**What the majority did instead.** The ayah continues: *those who did wrong pursued the enjoyment of good things of this worldly life, and were criminals.* Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning they continued in their ways of disobedience and evils and did not heed the protesting of those righteous people, until the torment suddenly seized them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it the same way — they went for the luxuries of the material world and turned into compulsive sinners.

Notice the order Ibn Kathir gives: the enjoyments they pursued, the protests they refused to heed, and then the sudden seizure. The deafness sits in the middle. Something had already been given away before the end came.

## Ayah 117: the rule behind every ruin

*And your Lord would never destroy the towns wrongfully, while their people were doers of good.*

Ibn Kathir reads this as a statement of Allah's perfect justice: He does not destroy any town except that it has wronged itself, and no correctional punishment or torment comes to any town except that its people were wrongdoers. He supports it with two other ayat — *We wronged them not, but they wronged themselves* (11:101), and *And your Lord is not at all unjust to His servants* (41:46). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the same principle in the sharpest terms: the probability of injustice and oppression does not exist with Allah; those destroyed deserved being destroyed.

**Two readings of "doers of good".** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān first takes *muṣliḥūn*, "people good in their ways", to mean *believing Muslims* — Allah does not destroy a town unjustly while its people are believers.

It then reports a second reading from some early commentators: that *ẓulm* (injustice) in this ayah means *shirk* — ascribing partners to Allah in His pristine divinity — and that *muṣliḥūn* refers to people who, despite being idolaters and disbelievers, are good in their morals and dealings: they do not hurt or cause pain to anyone, they do not lie, they do not cheat.

On that second reading, the ayah says something sobering. The punishment of *this world* does not fall on a people simply for being idolaters and disbelievers — unless they also spread disorder in the land by their very deeds and morals. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the causes the Qurʼān gives for the ruin of the earlier peoples were always particular evil *deeds*: the people of Nūḥ (peace be upon him) caused him all sorts of pain; the people of Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) spread disorder by weighing and measuring short; the people of Lūṭ (peace be upon him) took to the worst type of evil act; the people of Mūsā and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them) oppressed their prophets. Bare disbelief and shirk do not bring down the punishment of this world; the punishment for that, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is the everlasting punishment of the fire of Hell.

From this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, some scholars have said: **countries and governments can survive with disbelief and shirk, but they cannot survive with injustice and oppression.**

## What this asks of us

Ibn Kathir draws the practical conclusion directly out of ayah 116. Because the earlier generations lacked such a group, Allah commanded this noble Ummah always to keep among it those who command the good and forbid the evil — quoting *Let there arise out of you a group of people inviting to all that is good, enjoining righteousness and forbidding evil. And it is they who are the successful* (3:104).

He then reports that the Prophet ﷺ said that when people see an evil and do not change it, it is likely that Allah will cover them with His punishment. (Ibn Kathir introduces this simply as something related in a ḥadīth, without naming the collection, so it is given here exactly as he gives it.)

That is the warning of ayah 116 turned around and pointed at us. The lament was not over how many sinners a nation had, but over the people of sense who should have spoken and were not there.

## Ayat 118–119: why people never agree

*And if your Lord had so willed, He could surely have made mankind one Ummah, but they will not cease to disagree.*

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is informing us here that He is able to make all of mankind one nation, whether upon belief or upon disbelief — as He says elsewhere, *And had your Lord willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them together* (10:99). Then He tells us what will happen instead: people will always differ in religions, creeds, beliefs, opinions and sects.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the wisdom in this. Had it been Allah's will, He would have made all human beings accept Islam by force, and no difference would have remained among them at all. But such are the dictates of His wisdom that in this world Allah does not compel anyone to do anything. He has instead entrusted man with a kind of choice, under which he may do whatever good or bad he wishes. Then, human temperaments differ, ways differ and deeds differ — and the outcome is that there will always be some who keep at loggerheads against the true faith, with the exception of those whom Allah has blessed with His mercy: those who have been following the noble prophets.

**Which "difference" is being blamed?** This is an important qualification, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic about it. "Difference" in this place means hostility and opposition to the true faith and to the teachings of the prophets. It does *not* include the difference based on *ijtihād* — the disciplined effort of qualified scholars to derive rulings — which has been inevitable among the religious authorities and jurists of Islam, an ongoing process since the period of the Companions. That kind of difference is not contrary to divine mercy; it is in fact the very dictate of Allah's wisdom and mercy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that those who have used this ayah to declare the differences among the mujtahid imāms to be counter to mercy have themselves done something counter to the context of the ayah, and counter to the consistent practice of the Companions and those who followed them.

So the ayah is not a rebuke of scholarly disagreement — and on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, using it as one gets the ayah backwards.

## "Except those shown mercy by your Lord"

Ayah 119 opens with the exception, and Ibn Kathir explains who it covers: those who have received the mercy of Allah by following the Messengers — those who adhere to what they are commanded in the religion by the Messengers of Allah. That, he says, has always been their characteristic, until the coming of the finality of the prophets and messengers, Muhammad ﷺ; and those who received Allah's mercy after him are those who followed him, believed in him and supported him, and so succeeded by achieving happiness in this life and the Hereafter.

Ibn Kathir identifies them with the Saved Sect mentioned in the ḥadīth recorded in the *Musnad* and *Sunan* collections, noting that its routes of transmission all strengthen each other. In these narrations the Prophet ﷺ said that the Jews split into seventy-one sects, the Christians into seventy-two, and this nation will split into seventy-three, all of them in the Fire except one sect. When the Companions asked who they were, he said: *the sect that is upon what my Companions and I are upon.* Ibn Kathir notes that al-Ḥākim recorded this narration in his *Mustadrak* with that additional wording.

The measure given is not a party name or a label. It is a question: is this what the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions were upon?

## The decree behind it all

*and for that did He create them. And the Word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "Surely, I shall fill Hell with jinn and men all together."*

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is informing us that He precedes everything in His preordainment and decree, by His perfect knowledge and penetrating wisdom. The result of that decree is that, of those He created, some deserve Paradise and some deserve the Hellfire, and that He will fill the Hellfire with both mankind and jinn. As Ibn Kathir closes it: His is the profound evidence and the perfect wisdom.

This is why the passage does not end in despair over human stubbornness. The differing of people is not chaos; on Ibn Kathir's reading it runs inside a decree that is knowing and wise.

**The debate of Paradise and the Fire.** Ibn Kathir cites here a ḥadīth recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Paradise and the Hellfire debated. Paradise said, "None will enter me except the weak and despised of the people." The Hellfire said, "I have inherited the haughty and the arrogant people." Then Allah said to Paradise: *You are My mercy, and I grant mercy with you to whoever I wish.* And He said to the Hellfire: *You are My torment, and I take vengeance with you upon whoever I wish. I will fill each one of you.* However, Paradise will always have more bounties, to such an extent that Allah will create more creatures to dwell in it and enjoy its extra bounties. The Hellfire will keep saying, "Are there any more?" — until the Lord of Might places His Foot over it, and then it says: "Enough, enough, by Your might!"

Notice how the ḥadīth names the two: Paradise is Allah's *mercy*, and the Fire is His *torment*. And of the two, the one still described as having more to give, after all its people have entered, is Paradise.

## Living it

**Keep your baqiyyah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point about the word is worth carrying around: reason and insight are called a person's *remnant* because they are the dearest thing he has, the thing he parts with last. The ayah's whole lament is that in those nations, this was the thing that had gone missing.

**Say something.** Ibn Kathir's reading is that the very reason this Ummah was commanded to keep among it those who enjoin good and forbid evil is the gap that ruined the generations before. And the few who filled that gap in earlier nations are named, in the same ayah, as the ones Allah saved.

**Do not confuse decency with safety, or difference with disaster.** On the reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays from some early commentators, a society's survival in this world tracks its justice and its dealings, while the punishment for disbelief and shirk is the fire of the Hereafter. And ayah 118 teaches that people will differ until the end — the exception is mercy, and mercy is described as belonging to those who follow the Messenger ﷺ.

And Allah, Pure and High, knows best.

passages.title: Why these stories are told; wait and worship
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** After a whole sūrah of prophets and the peoples who rejected them, Allah now tells His Messenger ﷺ *why* He told him all of it — and then hands him the posture to hold: keep working, keep waiting, worship Allah, and rely on Him. Ayah 120 gives the purpose of the stories; ayat 121–122 are the parting word to those who will not believe; ayah 123 closes the sūrah — and closes the argument — by pointing to the One who knows everything hidden and to whom every affair returns.

What holds the four together is a single movement: *this is why you were told the stories → so this is how you now stand → and this is the One in whose hands the outcome sits.*

## Ayah 120: the stories were told to steady a heart

"And all that We relate to you of the news of the Messengers is in order that We may make strong and firm your heart thereby."

The purpose is stated in the ayah itself — *mā nuthabbitu bihi*, "that by which We make [your heart] firm." Not for entertainment, and not left to the reader to guess: Allah names the effect He intends these accounts to have on the heart that receives them.

Ibn Kathir unpacks it as Allah saying to him: *We relate all of these stories to you concerning what happened with the Messengers who came before you with their nations.* And he lists what the stories actually contain:

- **an explanation of what transpired in their arguments and disputes** — the confrontations between those Messengers and their peoples;
- **how the Prophets were all rejected and harmed** — *all* of them, none exempted;
- **how Allah helped His party of believers and disgraced His enemies, the disbelievers.**

Then Ibn Kathir gives the purpose in the Prophet's ﷺ own terms: "in order to make your heart firm and so that you may take an example from your brothers who passed before you of the Messengers."

*Your brothers.* That word carries the weight of the whole sūrah. The Messenger ﷺ, rejected and harmed by his own people, is not an anomaly — he stands in a line of brothers who each met the same rejection and each saw Allah help His party of believers. That is the comfort the stories were sent to give.

## "And in this has come to you the truth"

The ayah continues: *"And in this has come to you the truth, as well as an admonition and a reminder for the believers."*

What is "this"? Ibn Kathir reports the view of **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and a group of the Salaf** — and says plainly, "it is the correct view" — that *this* refers to **this Sūrah itself**: Sūrah Hūd, the sūrah just read.

His explanation: "This comprehensive Sūrah contains the stories of the Prophets and how Allah saved them, and the believers along with them, and how He destroyed the disbelievers. There has come to you stories of truth and true events in this Sūrah."

So three things arrive in one package, and they land differently on different people:

1. **The truth (*al-ḥaqq*).** In Ibn Kathir's words, "stories of truth and true events" — not moral fables, but what actually happened, as Allah relates it.
2. **An admonition** — one, in Ibn Kathir's words, "that prevents the disbelievers." A warning meant to stop a man before he walks the road the destroyed nations walked.
3. **A reminder** which "causes the believers to reflect." Not new information for them; a re-awakening of what they already know and keep forgetting.

The same sūrah does three jobs at once: it steadies the Prophet ﷺ, it warns the rejecter, it stirs the believer. And since the ayah names the believers as recipients of that reminder, a believer reading these accounts today is reading them for the purpose they were given.

## Ayat 121–122: "Persist in your ways — and wait"

"And say to those who do not believe: 'Act according to your ability and way, We are acting. And you wait! We too are waiting.'"

Ibn Kathir is careful about the tone: Allah "commands His Messenger ﷺ to say to those who disbelieve in what he has come with from his Lord, **by way of warning**." This is not a shrug, and it is certainly not "you have your truth and I have mine." It is a challenge, and Ibn Kathir marks it as a warning.

**"Act according to your ability" (*iʿmalū ʿalā makānatikum*)** — Ibn Kathir glosses: "This means upon your path and your way." Do everything you can from where you stand. Exhaust it.

**"We are acting" (*innā ʿāmilūn*)** — "This means that we are upon our path and our way (Islam)." The reply is deliberately parallel. Two parties, two roads, both fully committed, both working.

**"And you wait! We too are waiting" (*wa-ntaẓirū innā muntaẓirūn*)** — here Ibn Kathir supplies the meaning from another ayah: *"And you will come to know for which of us will be the (happy) end in the Hereafter. Certainly the wrongdoers will not be successful"* (6:135).

Notice the posture the Prophet ﷺ is given: both imperatives together — *keep acting* and *wait*. The waiting is not idleness; the one waiting is, by the same command, still working. And it is waiting with a known answer, since the meaning Ibn Kathir attaches to it is that they *will* come to know which side the good end belongs to. That is one of the most practically useful stances in the Qur'ān for anyone doing right in an environment where wrong keeps winning.

### How the waiting ended

Ibn Kathir does not leave the challenge hanging. He closes it with what followed: "Verily, Allah fulfilled His promise to His Messenger ﷺ, helped him and aided him. He made His Word uppermost (victorious), and the word of those who disbelieved lowly and disgraced. Allah is truly the Most Mighty, Most Wise."

The command to wait came first; the fulfilment came after. We read the words already knowing how the waiting was answered — which is itself part of the heart-steadying that ayah 120 promised.

### A note carried alongside this passage, on ayah 118

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** attaches to this closing section a discussion of an earlier ayah of the sūrah — ayah 118, "had your Lord willed, He would have made all the people a single community." Its point there: had Allah willed, "He would have made all human beings accept Islam by force," and no difference would have remained among them. "But such are the dictates of His wisdom that, in this world, Allah Taʿālā does not compel anyone to do something. Instead, He has entrusted man with a kind of choice under which he could do whatever good or bad he wishes to do." From that entrusted choice, "human temperaments differ, ways differ and deeds differ," and so "there always will be some people who would keep at loggerheads against the true faith" — except those whom Allah has blessed with His mercy, meaning those who follow the noble prophets.

**And a guardrail with it.** Because that ayah speaks of people "differing," some have used it to condemn all disagreement among Muslims. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān rejects that directly: the "difference" meant there "means hostility and opposition to the true faith and the teachings of prophets." Difference arising from *ijtihād* — the disciplined effort of a qualified scholar to derive a ruling — which "is inevitable among religious authorities and jurists of Islam, an ongoing process since the period of the Ṣaḥābah, is not included under this purview, nor is it contrary to Divine mercy. In fact, it is the very dictate of Allah's wisdom and mercy." Those who used that verse to declare the differences among the Mujtahid Imāms contrary to mercy, it says, argued against both the context of the verse and "the consistent practice of the Ṣaḥābah and Tābiʿīn."

## Ayah 123: where every affair returns

"And to Allah belongs the *Ghayb* of the heavens and the earth, and to Him return all affairs (for decision). So worship Him and put your trust in Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do."

*Ghayb* is rendered here as the unseen — what is hidden in the heavens and the earth. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah "informs that He is the All-Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth and that unto Him is final return."

Then the consequences, in order:

**Every deed is returned to its doer.** Ibn Kathir: "He explains that everyone who does a deed, He will give them their deed (reward for it) on the Day of Reckoning."

**Nothing sits outside His authority.** "Unto Him belongs the creation and the command."

**Therefore two commands follow** — and it matters that they are commands, not observations. Ibn Kathir: "Then He, the Exalted, commands that He should be worshipped and relied upon, for verily, He is sufficient for whoever trusts and turns to Him."

That is the logic of the whole sūrah compressed into a line. If the unseen belongs to Allah, if all affairs return to Him for decision, if every deed is repaid — then the response asked for is worship joined to reliance. Worship is what you do; reliance is what you do about what you cannot do. Both were commanded together, and the promise attached is enormous: **He is sufficient for whoever trusts and turns to Him.**

### "And your Lord is not unaware of what you do"

The sūrah's final clause is often heard only as a warning to the sinner. Ibn Kathir hears it first as consolation to the Messenger ﷺ:

"The lies (of the disbelievers) against you O Muhammad are not hidden from Him. He is the All-Knower of the conditions of His creatures and He will give them the perfect recompense for their deeds in this life and the Hereafter. He will aid you and His party over the disbelievers in this life and in the Hereafter."

So on Ibn Kathir's reading, the last word of Sūrah Hūd is not only a threat hanging over the reader. It tells the Prophet ﷺ that nothing said against him escaped Allah's knowledge, that the recompense is coming in full, and that the aid is promised to him and to His party — in this life and the next. The warning to the wrongdoer sits inside the same sentence, because the perfect recompense named there is for everyone's deeds.

The Ibn Kathir material on this ayah ends with the words: "This is the end of the Tafsir of Surah Hud, and all praises and thanks are due to Allah."

## Living it

**Read the prophets' stories for what they were sent to do.** Ayah 120 states their purpose outright: to make a heart firm — and names the believers as those the same sūrah reminds. Read them when your faith feels exposed or outnumbered.

**Keep working and keep waiting — at the same time.** Ayat 121–122 give both imperatives together. Do not stop acting on your way because the outcome is delayed; the decision of every affair returns to Allah (ayah 123).

**Answer opposition with steadiness, not anxiety.** "We are acting… we are waiting" is spoken by someone told that the good end will be known. Ibn Kathir's closing note — that Allah fulfilled His promise and made His Word uppermost — is how that waiting was answered.

**Do not turn scholarly disagreement into the "difference" that is blamed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that the difference blamed is hostility to the true faith and the teachings of the prophets, not the *ijtihād* of qualified jurists, which it calls the very dictate of Allah's wisdom and mercy.

**Pair worship with reliance.** Ayah 123 commands both together. Worship Him with your effort; hand Him the result — "He is sufficient for whoever trusts and turns to Him."

**Live as one whose Lord is not unaware.** The lies spoken against His Messenger ﷺ were not hidden from Him, and every deed receives its perfect recompense. Both halves of that are in the sūrah's final words.
